en: Combined Edition of the Commentary on the Meaning of the "Universal Gate" Chapter of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Volume One.
*Avalokiteśvara Commentary Record*, Volume One.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Zhili of Siming during the Song Dynasty.
○ Translation of the Commentary, Part Two: First, the Explanation of the Title; Second, the Direct Explanation of the Title.
*Guanyin yi shu*, Scroll One. [Record] "Yi" (義) means "appropriateness.
It refers to explaining the scriptural text so that it becomes appropriate, as well as "principle" (*yili*). This is because...
The wise enter the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* and, within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*), perceive the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

By means of this principle, they interpret the text of the present sutra; "commentary" (*shu*) is a term for the thorough understanding of its meaning. Furthermore, the pronunciation of "shu" is "shū," which carries the sense of "unraveling" (*shū-tōng*) or "analyzing" (*shū-tiáo*).
II. The Proclaimer of the Record.
Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty; recorded by his disciple Guanding. II.
Explanation of the Text of the Commentary. Part One: Preliminary Division of Chapters and Sections. 1. Narration of the Three Stages of the Two Schools.

Since this text was separately excerpted from the great collection (*mahāvaipulya-sūtra*), some also divide the text into three sections: the initial inquiry regarding "going" as the introduction (*nidāna*);

the Buddha’s response regarding "going" as the main body (*śarīra*); and the section on "the earth" as the dissemination (*pariṇāmana*). Furthermore, others say that the portion where the Sūtra-author provides the introduction serves as the introduction;
the portion where Akṣayamati addresses the Buddha serves as the main body; and the section on "the earth" serves as the dissemination.
[Commentary] Since this fascicle was separately transmitted to the world by Master Xian (Dharmakṣema) during the Northern Liang period under Juqu Mengxun,
many lecturers from the Liang and Chen dynasties onward have divided the scriptural text into three sections, resulting in differences [in their interpretations].
II. Now, regarding the Master’s [teachings] below, he demonstrates the various types [of expositions] at Tiantai. First, a general clarification of the various types and the division of the text.
At times, the present Master also structures [the text] into three sections; at other times, he does not structure it into three sections, but simply divides it into three chapters:
1. The Question of Ajita (Wujinyi); 2. The Buddha’s Response; 3. The Praise of Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Chidi). Alternatively, it is divided into four chapters, as in [the third case].

Regarding the first four sections, they may be understood as benefiting from the "Chapter on Hearing," or divided into two parts consisting of the preceding and succeeding question-and-answer sessions;
these various chapter divisions are employed according to the reader's own preference. Second, if one follows the three-part topical outline below, it is as follows:
[The main body of the text follows] Regarding the second section, "If one proceeds below," this refers to the correct reliance upon the three-part topical outline.

If one were to divide this into sections of questions and answers, there would be two such pairs. The first pair of questions and answers clarifies the meaning of the Bodhi tree king’s secret benefits and so forth;
the second pair of questions and answers clarifies the meaning of the Universal Gate pearl king’s manifest benefits and so forth.
II. Regarding the preceding section, the second part is the formal explanation of the sūtra text. This is divided into three sections. First, the preceding question and answer.
This is further divided into two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Regarding the question, there are four parts: first, the time; second, the designation of the person;
third, the respectful demeanor; fourth, the actual inquiry.
At that time. [Section Two:
Following the Explanation, Part One] There are four initial inquiries: first, the season; second, the explanation of the literal meaning of the characters.
First, regarding "at that time" (*tasmim samaye*): the word *er* (爾) means "that" (*ji*).

II. The second [section] clarifies the two types of *siddhānta* (doctrinal tenets) as follows. First, the individual explanation of their characteristics has four parts. First is the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint).

This refers to the period after the exposition by Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣadatta*) of the East regarding the propagation of the sutra has concluded, and before the exposition by Avalokiteśvara of the West regarding the propagation of the sutra begins;
therefore, it says, "At that time."
[Commentary] In the east and west, [the teaching] was given according to the capacities and inclinations of the listeners.

Second, it may be that this section is for individuals, or it may be that the great assembly has already heard the sublime sound of the propagation of the sutra and their joy is complete; they are now ready to hear the exposition on Avalokiteśvara.
It is called "at that time" because it is the moment when wholesome thoughts arise in the mind.
[Commentary] Alternatively, there are those whose faculties and dispositions have already attained understanding of the world upon hearing the preceding chapter;
thus, having finished with joy, they now give rise to their past wholesome roots immediately upon hearing this chapter.
Third, it may be that this serves as an antidote for those below.

Alternatively, it may be that at the time when the assembly was harboring doubts regarding the benefits of the Dharma taught by the Sublime Sound (Ghoṣadatta), and those doubts had already been resolved, there remained further doubts concerning the virtues of Avalokiteśvara; since he is now resolving these very doubts, it is said [as follows].
At that time. [Commentary:
The resolution of doubt belongs to the category of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*), while the realization of principle belongs to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Now, following the resolution of matters, it corresponds to the third *kṣānti* (receptivity).
Fourth, it may be that this refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Alternatively, it may mean that at that time, the capacities of the assembly were such that upon hearing the Sublime Sound (*Ghoṣeśvara*), they immediately attained the Way—just as the bodhisattvas of the two lands attained the Way—and that eighty-four thousand had already awakened to the principle; because they still required to hear Avalokiteśvara [further], it says, "At that time."
[Commentary]: "The two lands" refers to the Pure Radiance Adorned Land and this land. Regarding the eighty-four thousand who followed the Sublime Sound:
in this land, they were the Flower Virtue [Bodhisattva] and forty-two thousand devaputras; by means of that bodhisattva's coming and going, they attained the Way.
Now, eighty thousand have resolved their minds and awakened, remaining with Avalokiteśvara.
II. Regarding "All Buddhas" and below, this generally clarifies the "all-encompassing.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, preach the Dharma not in vain; there are four *siddhānta* causes and conditions for which they preach.
Since this is precisely the time for expounding the four *siddhāntas*, it says, "At that time."
[Commentary]: The Tathāgata is like a drum; when the four capacities [of sentient beings] strike it like a mallet, there is sound, yet the sound does not arise in isolation.
Now is precisely the time for the four capacities to strike the Buddha.
Thus, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati—
II. Identifying the Person (in two parts): A. Explaining the Individual Name; B. The Middle Way in contrast to the Lesser Vehicle.
Regarding the first [part], identifying the person: this is Akṣayamati. He is named "Inexhaustible" because he is neither exhaustible nor inexhaustible;

he is called "inexhaustible" because, in contrast to the Lesser Vehicle which speaks of "exhaustion," he is so designated. The Lesser Vehicle clarifies "exhaustion" as a contrast to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
Because it gives rise to wisdom, extinguishes form, and exhausts the grasping at emptiness, it is called "inexhaustible" (*akṣaya*).

[Commentary] This name for the Bodhisattva is established based on realization; herein, one must necessarily avoid partiality. Now, the emphasis on "inexhaustibility" is specifically intended as an antidote to the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), which is a dharma of extinction.
It serves to manifest that the nature of the Middle Way is inexhaustible, whereas the Small Vehicle is characterized by exhaustion.
The "knowledge of the wise" refers to the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), vision, clarity, and awakening that arises when one reflects: "I have seen suffering; I have abandoned its origin;
I have realized its cessation; I have cultivated the path. The "knowledge of non-arising" refers to [the realization]: "I have seen suffering and shall not see it again;
I have abandoned its origin and shall not abandon it again; I have fully realized its cessation and shall not realize it again; I have cultivated the path."
Having already ceased further cultivation of such mindfulness, one attains at that time the outflow-free wisdom, vision, clarity, and awakening.
○ Second, the section beginning with "Furthermore" explains the perfect and complete illumination of the latter three truths; first, the general demonstration.

Furthermore, what is meant by "inexhaustible"? It is called inexhaustible because emptiness (*śūnyatā*) cannot be exhausted, the provisional (*prajñapti*) cannot be exhausted, and the middle (*madhyama*) cannot be exhausted.
○ Second, in the lower part of the *Dapin* (Large Chapter), there is a separate exposition in three parts; first, the perfect emptiness is inexhaustible.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Form itself is emptiness; it is not that form is extinguished to become empty. Because it is empty, it is inexhaustible.
[Commentary] To distinguish and analyze in order to reveal the essence, it says "form itself is emptiness. One should know that the essence of emptiness permeates the three vehicles of the Mahāyāna.

Generally speaking, merely realizing that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself empty is the "partial emptiness" (*ekadeśa-śūnyatā*). The Distinct and Perfect [teachings], however, are able to realize that even *nirvāṇa* is empty.
"Empty" refers to emptiness within this [state]. To depart from the partial (pradeśa) is to belong to the distinct; that which belongs to the partial is now within the perfect (pariniṣpanna).
Within the perfect, it is called "empty," and this emptiness is inexhaustible.
II. Furthermore, "Great" and below: The Perfect Provisional is Inexhaustible. Part One: Quoting the Sūtra to Show its Characteristics. Sub-part One: The *Mahāsaṃnipāta*.
Approximately eighty [verses] clarify the two types of provisional [teachings]. First, regarding what was practiced in his original land:

furthermore, according to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati explained that to the east, past worlds as numerous as the dust motes of ten Ganges-sands of lands, there is a land named Amoghadarśana and a Buddha named Samantabhadra.
It consists purely of bodhisattvas; there are no names for the two vehicles, and they practice only mindfulness.
The Buddha’s samādhi is neither extinguished nor born, and his mental activity does not emerge; it is equal and impartial like empty space. This is what is meant by mindfulness of the Buddha.
At the very moment one sees the Buddha, one is fully endowed with the six pāramitās and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

That is to say: not grasping at form is *dāna* (generosity); removing the characteristics of form is *śīla* (ethical discipline); contemplating the exhaustion of form is *kṣānti* (patience); and contemplating the quiescence of form is [the perfection of] *dhyāna* (meditation).
That is to say: diligence does not engage with form, dhyāna does not engage in conceptual proliferation regarding form, and this is prajñā.

[Commentary] This is the wondrous provisional [nature], which possesses the three contemplations: because it is not extinguished, it is provisional; because it is not produced, it is empty; because it does not emerge, it is the middle.
This is because it does not flow out toward the two extremes. When one contemplates the Buddha through this contemplation, one fully contemplates the three bodies (*trikāya*). Up to...
The stage of partial realization is called "seeing the Buddha," for all the Buddha-dharmas manifest before one without exception; here, only the six perfections are cited by way of illustration.
II. Subhūti and others establish the names based on the Dharma. Part One: Subhūti’s Question.
Śāriputra asked, "Who gave you the name 'Inexhaustible Intention'?
The second Bodhisattva replied:
"Because all dharmas—both causes, conditions, and their karmic fruits and retributions—are inexhaustible; because all dharmas cannot be exhausted."

Once the unsurpassed bodhicitta has been first generated, it is inexhaustible; just as space cannot be exhausted, how could the generation of the bodhicitta for the sake of all-knowledge ever be exhausted?

Since this generation of the mind is the cause for the inexhaustibility of the Buddhas' morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth, it is therefore inexhaustible.

Because one can exhaustively understand the inexhaustibility of the nature of sentient beings, the inexhaustibility of teaching and transforming sentient beings, and the inexhaustibility of the nature of all phenomena, this inexhaustibility is called the inexhaustibility of the bodhisattva’s resolve.

Furthermore, from the inexhaustibility of the *dānapāramitā* up to the inexhaustibility of *upāya*, there are eighty such inexhaustibilities; these eighty inexhaustibilities are all fully contained within it.
All Buddha-dharmas derive their name from this; thus he is named Akṣayamati (Inexhaustible Intention).

[Commentary] This fully manifests his vows and practices. Because his vows and practices are inexhaustible, the name is established here. Regarding the causes and conditions of the causal stage and the retribution of the resultant stage:

the "causes and conditions" refers to the arising of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*) upon which he establishes his vow; the "retribution" refers to suffering itself. For the sake of all beings and so forth, he relies on cessation (*nirodha*) to establish [his practice].

One vows by means of the fruit of Buddhahood—namely, all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) and the fivefold qualities (*pañca-dharma*)—to establish this vow based on the inferior nature of sentient beings in order to transform them in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because one knows these dharmas, it is said that "one generates the resolve" (*cittotpāda*); this refers to knowing that the vow is thus established.
Furthermore, based on the vow, one establishes practice; the myriad practices are all subsumed within the perfections (*pāramitā*), such as giving (*dāna*). This is what is meant by "proclaiming."
When the practice of the *pāramitās* reaches its fruition, because both aspiration and practice are characterized by non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), they become inexhaustible.
In total there are eight [sections]. The conclusion below summarizes that these aspirations and practices are all the *dharmadhātu*; therefore, they encompass all Buddha-dharmas.
Second, furthermore, the "Pure" and "Lower Pure" names clarify the provisional [nature] by means of the two truths.

Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* asks: "What is meant by 'exhaustion'? It means not exhausting existence (*bhava*). What is meant by 'non-exhaustion'? It means not abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
[Commentary]: Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are conventional and subject to exhaustion; unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are ultimate and inexhaustible.

Because the wisdom of the Lesser Vehicle is shallow, it exhausts the conditioned and abides in the unconditioned; thus, they return to the extinction of ashes. Perfect beings, however, contemplate the conventional as wondrous existence (*miyōu*), and therefore practice the myriad practices.
They contemplate the ultimate and are able to reach the truth that is not empty (*fukū-no-shin*); for this reason, they do not abide [in the unconditioned].
The three unconditioned states (asaṃskṛta) are like pits; therefore, both truths are eternally abiding and inconceivable, and because they are provisionally designated, they are called inexhaustible.
Third, the *Avataṃsaka* clarifies the provisional based on the ten treasuries (daśakośa).
The *Avataṃsaka* contains ten inexhaustible dharma-gates.
[Commentary] The new translation’s *Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries Sūtra* states that Bodhisattvas have ten kinds of treasuries which all Buddhas of the three periods of time teach:
namely, the treasury of faith, the treasury of precepts, the treasury of shame, the treasury of remorse, the treasury of learning, the treasury of giving, and the treasury of wisdom.
The treasury of mindfulness, the treasury of retention, the treasury of eloquence, and so forth, up to:

"These ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries have ten kinds of inexhaustibility that cause all bodhisattvas to reach ultimate enlightenment. What are the ten? Because they benefit all sentient beings;
because they are skillfully dedicated through original vows; because they are uninterrupted throughout all eons; because they pervade the entirety of space..."
Because all realms are fully awakened through the boundlessness of the mind; because one dedicates [merit] to the conditioned without attachment;
because the realm of a single thought-moment is the inexhaustibility of all phenomena; because the great vow-mind is immutable; because one skillfully grasps all *dhāraṇīs*;
because one is protected and remembered by all Buddhas; and because one understands that all phenomena are like illusions.
These are the ten kinds of inexhaustible dharmas that enable all worldly activities to attain the ultimate, inexhaustible great treasury. [Section] Two:
From "In this way" onwards, the sutra concludes by clarifying the provisional nature [of these teachings].
All such sutras clarify the inexhaustible intention by analyzing the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of all phenomena according to conventional designations. III.

Furthermore, as in the second section on the "Inexhaustibility within the Perfect [Nature]," there are four parts: first, citing the sutra to demonstrate the characteristics; fourth, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
To clarify this according to the Buddha-dharma, as the Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra states: "The form of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise so;
all dharmas are eternally abiding."
[Commentary] Because all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, there is no dharma that is not the center; because it is eternally abiding and eternally abiding, it is inexhaustible.
○ Second, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies the "center" (*madhya*) by way of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All dharmas tend toward the mind; they do not transcend this tendency. The mind is the dharma-realm;
thus, the mind is neither exhausted nor inexhaustible. This inexhaustibility is, for example, like that which is neither eternal nor impermanent—this is what constitutes the eternal."
[Commentary]: Because the essence of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is the great universal characteristic, all phenomena converge toward it;

just as when one grasps the main collar of a garment, all the hair and eyes follow, so too when one reaches the fundamental object, everything returns to the center. What phenomenon is not universal? Now, the specific mention of "mind" is intended to explain the meaning of the sutra:

the principle of the Dharma-realm must be a dual negation. It is called "inexhaustible" because while the name is partial, the meaning is complete; therefore, it is exemplified by the "true permanence."
In reality, there are no inverted views; now I shall explain that they are inexhaustible, being so both above and below.
Third, Vimalakīrti demonstrates that the extremes are themselves the middle.

Furthermore, Vimalakīrti says: "Whether dharmas are exhausted or not exhausted, they all possess the characteristic of inexhaustibility; this characteristic of inexhaustibility is precisely [the middle]."
Since this emptiness of emptiness has neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion, one knows that being neither exhausted nor non-exhausted is the true meaning of non-exhaustion.
[Commentary] Emptiness and existence, in their very essence, are all the perfect, central, and neutral nature; as they do not undergo change, how could there be exhaustion? This—

Because it exhausts the mental states of the two extremes, it is able to empty both the exhausted and the inexhaustible; thus, we know that the concluding summary below establishes that the Perfect Middle is the true inexhaustibility.
Chapter Four on the Four Great Elements clarifies that all dharmas are the Middle.
Furthermore, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Ignorance is like space and is inexhaustible, up to and including old age and death, which are like space and are inexhaustible;
form is inexhaustible, up to and including consciousness, which is inexhaustible."

[Commentary]: Since the entirety of cultivated evil is inherently evil, the statement that the twelve links of dependent origination and the five aggregates are each like emptiness—eternally abiding and all-pervasive—cannot be reconciled with the tenets of this school. This text remains unexplained.
○ Second, from "In this way" below, the sūtra concludes by clarifying the Middle Way.
Sūtras such as these all employ the principle of the Middle Way to designate it as "inexhaustible.
○ Third, from "Thoroughly penetrating" below, there are two parts concerning establishing names based on virtues; first, the actual establishment of the name.
Because he has thoroughly penetrated the Dharma of the three truths—emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—which are inexhaustible, he is named Bodhisattva Inexhaustible Intent (*Akṣayamati*).

[Commentary] The intent that is able to penetrate derives its name of "inexhaustibility" from the dharmas it penetrates. A student must understand that the intent is itself the three truths; there is no distinction between them.
Furthermore, the penetrated (the object) and the penetrating (the subject) are likewise non-dual. If it were otherwise, he would not be the Bodhisattva Inexhaustible Intent.
Second, it is also called "an example for all dharmas.
It is also called "the inexhaustible mind"; the meanings of consciousness, form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and so forth, are unspeakable and unspeakable, and cannot be fully recorded.
[Commentary: Since the five aggregates of mind and intellect, as well as all phenomena, are identical with the three truths, they all receive the designation "inexhaustible.
Section Two: Explaining the General Name. Part One: Translating the Name from Sanskrit.
"Bodhisattva" (菩薩) is called *mahābodhicittasattva* in foreign lands, which translates here as "sentient beings of the great path-mind.
○ Second, explaining the meaning by means of the flower [analogy], in two parts: first, explaining "sentient beings," in two parts: first, a general clarification of cause and effect.
The practitioner who begins with the mind is born from afflictions; those of the Two Vehicles are born from the fivefold Dharma-body;

the Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections are born from merit and virtue; and those of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings] are born from the Middle Way. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The body of the Tathāgata is not produced from a single cause or a single condition."

[Commentary] All those who can produce real dharmas and all those produced as provisional persons—from ordinary beings up to the most exalted individuals—without exception arise from a multitude of dharmas.
2. Specifically clarifying the Bodhisattva.
Because Bodhisattvas give rise to the various practices for the sake of the multitude, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*).
[Commentary: Because they arise from inexhaustible and manifold practices, they are termed "sentient beings.
Second, from "generating the mind" (*cittotpāda*) onwards, the remaining characters are explained.

Because they resolve their minds to seek Buddhahood, it is said that for the sake of the Great Way they benefit all beings; through the Way of the Dharma, they bring others to completion, or as some say, they bring sentient beings to completion.

[Commentary] Furthermore, based on the upward seeking and downward transforming, the previous [explanation] was given by means of the various practices arising and provisionally establishing a person; now, by means of...
The Way and its Dharma bring completion to other sentient beings.
○ Third, the extensive explanation is as in the separate [text].
The extensive explanation of the meaning of "bodhisattva" is as in the separate record.
III. The Threefold Rite of Reverence (Trividha-gaurava-vidhi). Part One: The Scriptural Text.
Regarding the threefold rite of reverence, there are three parts: first, rising; second, baring the right shoulder;
third, joining the palms. That is to say: rising from one’s seat, baring the right shoulder, and joining the palms toward the Buddha, one speaks as follows.

Regarding the second section, "Arising" (qǐ): the following provides a sequential commentary on the three [sections]. First is the explanation of "arising. There are two parts to this: first, the literal explanation.

As for "arising," the *Li* (Book of Rites) says: "When requesting instruction, one rises; when requesting to undertake a task, one rises. Because the Bodhisattva possesses both of these two modes of conduct toward the Buddha, it is said that he "arises."

[Commentary]: "Ritual" refers here to the *Quli* (Etiquette and Ceremonies). It says there: "When requesting instruction, one rises; when requesting further elucidation, one rises. Master Zheng’s commentary states: "This is to honor the teacher and revere the Way.
"Rising" means, as it does today, to lift the hem of one's robe and step forward to request instruction. "Instruction" (*ye*) refers to the chapters and scrolls of a text;

"further elucidation" (*yi*) refers to a desire for the teacher to explain more clearly when what has been received is not fully understood. Now, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati wishes to request [instruction from] Avalokiteśvara.
Because the activity of benefiting others is the practice of a bodhisattva intended to benefit one’s own mind, [the Buddha] rose from his seat.
II. The Exegesis of the Contemplation (in three parts): First, the arising discussed in terms of emptiness.
Regarding the exegesis of the contemplation: because a bodhisattva constantly cultivates the practice of detachment, "arising" is also said to be in accord with the emptiness of all phenomena.
Emptiness itself is the seat; because one is unstained by and unattached to this emptiness, it is said that one "arises.

[Commentary] This passage has two meanings: first, it clarifies that the contemplation of emptiness does not cling to any phenomena; second, it clarifies that the contemplation of emptiness itself does not cling to emptiness, and for this reason, it is called "arising."
Second, furthermore, from "The Bodhisattva... onwards, it is discussed in terms of conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

Furthermore, although the principle of emptiness in which the Bodhisattva dwells is fundamentally without arising, because he takes pity on sentient beings and benefits them according to their capacities, it is said that [the mind] arises.
[Commentary] This refers to manifesting various dignified postures (*īryāpatha*) while remaining in the meditative concentration of neither-arising-nor-extinction (*anirodhānutpāda-samādhi*).
Thirdly, regarding the middle and lower [capacities], it is discussed in terms of arising from the Middle Way.
Furthermore, the quiescence of the Middle Way is neither arising nor non-arising; yet, being able to arise and able to not arise, it is an arising that is without arising.
"Arising" means that arising itself is the true mark (dharmatā), and it is called "arising" because it is the true mark of sentient beings as well.

[Commentary] Since the Middle Way’s negation and illumination are both free from mutual dependence and opposition, whether there is arising or non-arising, there is nothing that is not the Middle Truth.
Thus, the illumination within negation is called "the arising of non-arising. This arising is able to spontaneously give rise to the Middle Truth, and it is also able to cause others to do so.
Arousing the genuine reality within.
○ Second, the partial uncovering [of the shoulder] and below explains the patriarchs in two parts; first, the explanation through events, with the first part concerning the Western Land (India).
Regarding "partial uncovering of the right shoulder": in foreign lands, baring the shoulder is a mark of respect; exposing the right side indicates the convenience of holding and making offerings.
This table clarifies the ritual for a disciple performing service for his teacher; therefore, baring the shoulder (袒) is regarded as an act of reverence.
○ Second, regarding this region:
in this region, baring the shoulder is considered an act of insolence; however, in antiquity there was Xu Jia, who bared his flesh (肉袒) to apologize to Zhang Yi, exposing both shoulders.
The thigh; in this context, it is not invariably a case of arrogance.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement that "Xu Jia apologized to Zhang Yi," it should properly be "Zhang Lu"; this is an error in the character.
Originally, Mang Sui was a man of Wei who first served Wei and, together with the Grand Minister Xu Jia, was sent as an envoy to Qi. Qi [treated] Sui...
Because Xian had privately rewarded him with gold, jade, oxen, and wine, Su Jia became jealous and enraged;

he sent [an agent] back to slander Zou Yan to Wei Qi, the Chancellor of Wei. Wei Qi was furious and beat him until his ribs were broken and his teeth were shattered, then threw him into a latrine and covered him with bedding.
Zou Yan did not die; he sought out a guard and had him remove him.
Having managed to escape, Xu changed his name to Zhang Lu and followed the Qin envoy Wang Ji into the state of Qin.
Upon meeting King Zhao, the King was pleased with him and appointed him as a Guest Minister (Keqing). He was subsequently promoted to Left Chancellor.

Later, when Xu Ju became an envoy to Qin, Xu (Zhang Lu) went out in humble attire and encountered Ju on the road leaning on a staff. Seeing him, Ju was greatly startled and asked, "Have you returned?"
Jia said, "I am a fugitive; I have barely escaped death. How would I dare to speak with the state of Qin?
He asked Jia again, "Do you know Zhang Jun, the Chancellor of Qin? Jia replied, "My master may also gain access to him.
Jia said, "Now I wish to use you as an intermediary to request an audience with the Chancellor. Thereupon, they went together to the gate of the Chancellor's residence.
The gatekeeper rose in alarm, his expression stern as he grew suspicious; Jia entered but did not emerge. When Jia questioned the gatekeeper, he learned it was the Chancellor of Qin;
turning pale with fear, he removed his cap, bared his chest, and requested entry to offer his apologies. Jia then rebuked and scolded him.
When Jia’s mission returned, Jia said, "Report to the Lord of Wei on my behalf that you must execute Wei Qi; otherwise—"

The wisdom true body (*jñāna-dharmakāya*) also possesses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); the five aggregates of the causes and conditions for response and transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) also exist;

[Commentary]: Delusion differs from awakening, yet the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is fundamentally identical; how then could there be any difference between ordinary beings and sages? It is simply that the sage has emerged from the entanglements (*saṃyojana*), whereas sentient beings remain immersed in defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
Within this state of defilement, the aggregates of nature give rise to the aggregates of birth-and-death, which act as the "stimulator" (*kāraka*).

Consequently, when the sage emerges from the entanglements, the aggregates of reality give rise to the provisional aggregates to act as the "respondent" (*pratibhāka*). If, moreover, the nature itself were to respond, one would return directly to the Truth (*tattva*).

Therefore, the two palms represent the present; by joining them now, one intends for the practitioner to immediately perceive that the phenomenal aspect (shī-yin) merges with the noumenal aspect (xìng-yin).

II. Clarifying the Seven Difficulties as Posited by the Opponent. Part One: Clarifying the Sequence. First, establishing the sequence provisionally:
since the opponent has already set forth the sequence of the seven difficulties, we now respond to them accordingly. Entering fire would result in being scorched.
The anxiety over the loss of life is the most urgent and grave; therefore, it is placed first. Drowning in water is slightly less immediate than being consumed by fire.

Although the rākṣasīs are violent—as the sūtra says there were five hundred rākṣasīs who took five hundred castaways as wives, and while they enjoyed their offspring for a long period of time, they eventually devoured them all—this is still less immediate than the peril of the King of Hell.

Furthermore, it is not the case that one is immediately captured and executed; rather, the crimes are investigated to determine their reality or falsehood. If they are real, there is punishment; if they are false, there is pardon.
This is unlike ghosts, which indiscriminately seize and devour all at once; thus, it is also different from rākṣasas. When ghosts come to take [a person], there is no fixed target for their seizure;

harm is encountered only when one's merit declines, and if one escapes, one may be spared. This is unlike the royal law, which definitively judges between life and death. Furthermore, it is different from the perils of kingship.

Furthermore, being bound with shackles and fetters, one does not consider the loss of life, but suffers only the hardship of confinement; this is slightly less severe than the resentment of ghosts or bandits seeking treasure.
Once the treasure has been delivered, the matter is finished. If one can employ humble words and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one may escape the bandits.
Such is the sequence of events in this case.
[Commentary] This sequence from heavy to light follows a single progression.

Regarding the "penetrating clarity" (tongming) of seven and six:

Just as it is difficult for seven people to dwell together harmoniously, and seven are considered a source of difficulty, here the seven difficulties and so forth are generally employed to symbolize the six.
The elements of fire, water, and wind represent the three types [of afflictions] within the body; swords, staves, shackles, and fetters represent the element of earth;

[Commentary] The Sūtra clarifies that the seven calamities do not merely refer to external events; rather, they are explained through contemplation as mutually inclusive across the three vehicles.
If there were nothing to be symbolized, they could not encompass the profound depths. Therefore, by means of the seven calamities, six types of external elements are symbolized:

water, fire, and wind represent the three internal [elements]; the sword, the chain, and the hard obstruction represent the internal earth element; and kings and other sentient beings symbolize the seeds of consciousness.
Although the three-thousandfold world system is not itself the direct object of negation, it serves as the basis for that negation and can thus represent internal emptiness.

II. Now, to establish the following [section], there are two parts in accordance with the principle: first, responding to hardships by fulfilling one's vows; second, the three vehicles.

Now, this establishes the King-Samādhi (Rājasamādhi), which is quiescent yet constantly illuminating. "Sentient beings" refers to those drifting upon the waters of retribution, which are termed "faculties" (*indriya*);

"responding to circumstances" refers to the compassion that saves them from the water of karmic fruition. "Precepts and concentration" refers to the compassion that saves them from the water of evil karma; "the three contemplations" refer to the compassion [that saves them from] the water of [deluded] views.
[Commentary]: By gradually practicing and suddenly realizing [enlightenment], one constantly mirrors the Dharma-realm.

Through ten successive opportunities for spiritual resonance, one vows, at every stage within the causal ground, to ensure that all beings drifting in the waters of the three obstacles attain liberation.
Thus, they are rescued from the waters of affliction, and all simultaneously achieve deliverance.
II. Second, citing scriptures from below the section "Like a Flower" to establish the proof, in two parts: first, the proof.
As clarified in the thirty-eighth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when Sudhana arrives at the country of Samudramukha, the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha preaches the *Samantacakṣus Sūtra* for him, saying:
"For twelve years, I have constantly contemplated this ocean; it gradually becomes deeper and deeper, and great bodies dwell within it."

Having observed the accumulation of rare jewels in this manner, he then saw a great lotus flower arise from the bottom of the ocean, adorned by immeasurable devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings.

Upon the flower was a Buddha with boundless marks and signs of excellence, who extended his right hand and stroked my head, preaching the *Puyan Jing* (Universal Eye Sūtra) for twelve hundred years; in a single day, he bestowed upon me incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) teachings.

The chapters are immeasurable and boundless; even if one were to use the waters of the ocean as ink and the Mount Sumeru mountains piled together as pens to write this sutra, one could not exhaust it.

[Commentary] Relying on the metaphorical sea to contemplate the sea of the three obstacles, "twelve years" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), which are gradually...
The ten virtues and ten contemplations of the ocean of ever-deepening insight are accomplished; the arising of the great lotus flower manifests the wondrous realm.
The adornment by devas and nāgas signifies the possession of wondrous power and function. The presence of the Buddha’s marks and signs means one constantly beholds Vairocana.
The extending of the right hand represents the response of expedient wisdom; the touching of one’s crown represents the resonance of true wisdom. Thus, through this resonance—

The Way should be manifested through mutual interaction, for this is the beginning where the fundamental and the derivative are unified. To speak of the *Puyan Jing* (Universal Eye Sutra) is to attain the dharma of the fruition within its divisions.
That which one receives in a single day cannot be fully exhausted; it is because the dust of a single thought-moment manifests the sutra-scrolls of the great thousandfold world-system.
II. The Conclusion: It should be known that the Dharma-gate of Water encompasses all phenomena, just as the letter "A" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* contains all meanings.
Because Avalokiteśvara has long since attained thorough penetration of the Dharma-gate of Water, he is able to respond universally to all waters.
[Answer: It is difficult. [Commentary: Since the letter A possesses all meanings, one should know that it is also a Dharma-gate of the Middle Way;
however, because it is associated with the path of teaching, one knows only this single aspect.
II. Furthermore, below [the section on] "Sudden" (dùn), there are two parts; first, the sudden cultivation (*sudden-practice*).
Furthermore, regarding the Dharma-gate of the fundamental practice of the Perfect Contemplation (*yuan-guan*), wherein non-referential compassion universally responds to all things:

one contemplates the Water-Syllable Gate (*āp-dvāra*) such that the ten Dharma-realms enter the Water-Syllable, and this entry does not exceed it. Since even water itself cannot be apprehended, how much less so [the realms]?
When one considers that the waters of the ten realms of existence and non-existence are ultimately unattainable even as conventional truth, how could there be going or not going?
This simultaneous negation reveals the Middle Way, the ultimate truth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "waters of the ten realms and destinies," because water represents the Dharma-realm which encompasses all phenomena exhaustively, it is called a "destiny" (*gati*).

Since both the "one who goes" (*gantṛ*) and the "place to which one goes" (*gantavya*) are established, this corresponds to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). As for the phrase "the waters are still equal": the entirety of the waters that constitute the destination are the nature itself;
since no characteristics can be apprehended and there is nothing to be gone toward, how could there be one who goes? Thus, both the subject and object [of going] are [empty].
Emptiness is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). What does this mean? Since even water cannot be found, there is no place of entry (*praveśa*);
when the place of entry is cut off, the act of entering is naturally forgotten. Thus, by means of "double negation," the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) is revealed.
These three truths share the same single *dharmatā*; they are three while being one, and one while being three—an inconceivable mystery.
II. Regarding the phrase "In this way," the following section should be divided into two parts: first, clarifying that which should not be responsive yet is responsive.
When one contemplates the ten dharma-realms and the three truths within the single character "water" in this manner, the non-conditioned great compassion immediately arises;
because it universally permeates the sentient beings of the three truths and ten dharma-realms, it is able to respond perfectly to all.
[Commentary] The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "If compassion exists, does not exist, both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist, it is called the Tathāgata’s compassion.

Is this not the arising of compassion through the three truths? In the previous general objection, it was stated that when sentient beings of the ten realms suffer and call upon the name, the Bodhisattva immediately contemplates their cries and they all attain liberation.
If one does not contemplate the ten realms as empty, provisional, and the Middle, how [can this be]?
To be able to leave all suffering behind at once is precisely because the three truths are the fundamental nature of birth and the source of the fruits of sagehood;
since they possess no dual essence, it is only through compassion of identical substance that one can thoroughly uproot [suffering].
II. Clarifying the division within the undivided.
If one contemplates through analysis: one uses sixteen samādhis to rescue [beings] from the waters of karmic retribution; twenty-four samādhis to rescue them from the waters of evil karma;
and twenty-five samādhis to rescue those of the Two Vehicles from their entry into emptiness—whether by the Shared, Distinct, or Complete teachings.
Using the waters of the outflows and so forth, one rescues those of the Separate Teaching who have emerged into the provisional through twenty-five samādhis,
ensuring they remain unstained by the moisture within the outflows; using the twenty-five samādhis, one rescues those of the Perfect Teaching who have entered the Middle Way,
such that all [afflictions] are simultaneously liberated from the flowing waters of ignorance.

[Commentary] The general meaning is the same as what was explained previously regarding the "peril of fire. Here, the four flows (*catur-ogha*) are contrasted with the various stages to demonstrate how the four teachings enter emptiness and depart from the flow of existence (*bhava-srotas*), and so forth.
Regarding the two flows of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and desire (*kāma*): the "flow of existence" refers to being unstained by the moisture [of attachment].
Although the provisional (*prajñapti*) refutes emptiness, one does not yet cling to existence because both flows are present; thus, it should be understood that the provisional reveals emptiness.
Furthermore, the meaning of the "Contemplation of Equality" (Samatā-vipaśyanā) is widely renowned; its significance lies herein in the destruction of ignorance, as has been explained previously.

III. The Peril of Rākṣasas (2): First, the enumeration of the topical categories.

Regarding the third, the peril of rākṣasas, it is also threefold: first, the word-by-word commentary; second, the application to actual events; and third, the interpretive explanation through contemplation.
II. Explanation according to the sections (suí-mén-shì): Part One, Adhering to the Text (tiē-wén). This is further divided into two:

1. Explaining the difficulties; 2. Concluding the names. Within the explanation of the difficulties, there are five parts: 1. Stating the number; 2. Clarifying the reasons for encountering the difficulties;
3. Suffering the difficulties; 4. Clarifying the capacity (jī); 5. Clarifying the response.
If there are hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions of sentient beings who, seeking treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral,
amber, and pearls, enter the great ocean; and if a black wind should blow their ship and cast it adrift into the land of the rākṣasa demons—
if among them even a single person should invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—
All these people have attained liberation from the perils of the rākṣasas; for this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara.
[Section on the Number of People] (Part Two: Following the Explanation). First, clarifying the perils (five parts). First, citing the number. (Two parts). First, explaining the number of people.

Regarding the number of people, the mention of "hundreds of thousands" is a general figure and does not definitively determine the exact quantity. It clarifies that when entering the sea to seek treasures, the companionship formed is indefinite;
yet, although the number is not fixed, one must never go alone, which is why "hundreds of thousands" is cited.
[Commentary] Whether there be a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred million, because one must board a great ship to cross the sea,
it is said that they form a company and cannot go alone.
○ Second, from "The Wise and the Foolish" onwards, it clarifies entering the sea.
The *Xiányú jīng* (Sutra on the Wise and the Foolish) states: "Agriculture yields a hundredfold; commerce yields a thousandfold; official service yields ten thousandfold;
but entering the sea and returning safely yields immeasurable multiples.
Section Two: The Causes for Encountering Adversity at Sea. Part One: The Correct Explanation of the Causes for Adversity. Sub-part One: Proving that Wind is Not the Primary Cause.
[Objection: Difficult.

Next, as for the "encountering wind" being a calamity, this is based on the evidence provided in the subsequent text. If we were to exclude the wind from being a primary calamity here, the subsequent text would state:
"All shall attain liberation from the calamity of the rākṣasas. How could this not refer exclusively to the calamity of the rākṣasas?

[Commentary] Because the ancient masters established the "wind" as one of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), based on the phrasing of the text, it constitutes only the difficulty of being a hungry ghost (*preta*).
Second, the two difficulties [arise] from the following; the difficulty of wind arises from below.
As for the difficulty arising from the "proper cause" (*yoniśas*), what is it that constitutes this cause? It is solely due to the wind. Regarding the difficulty of falling [into the ocean]:
when one enters the sea to seek treasures because of a craving for precious jewels, one encounters the wind; thus, the wind is the cause of the calamity of falling.
Because the disaster of the wind is so urgent, the wind is the cause of the falling calamity.
[Commentary]: If one traces these back step by step, they are all difficulties arising from various causes; among these, the cause of wind (*vāta*) is the most urgent.
Therefore, the sutra text specifically mentions only "wind.
○ Second, regarding the seven treasures below, there is a retrospective explanation of the precious objects in two parts: first, distinguishing between the genuine and the counterfeit.
The seven treasures are the true jewels, while this pearl is a counterfeit jewel; furthermore, the wish-fulfilling jewel is the most supreme.
Now, when it says "equal," it means equal to all other jewels, both superior and inferior.
2. Showing what resembles the real.
The *Loutan jing* (Louván jīng) states that within the great ocean there are seven kinds of semblance-jewels and one hundred and twenty kinds of true jewels.

○ Third, regarding the "black wind" (*kālaka-vāta*) below, there is a further explanation of the characteristics of the wind in two parts: first, the interpretations of others; third, the initial establishment by the former masters. First, the interpretations of others. First, the establishment by the former masters.
Regarding "black wind" (*kṛṣṇavāta*): the old [translation] states that it is so called because it is a colorless wind that blows black sand.
○ Second, "There is a person... and below is the refutation by another. Someone objects, saying:
"In the sand there is no boat, and in the water there is no sand; it is not that black sand is being blown [there], but rather..."
It is merely blowing black clouds.
○ Third, now we shall return to the standard objection:
"If there are no clouds in the water and no boat in the clouds, how can one strike the sand to take [the fish]?"
If wind and clouds can blow away black clouds, for what reason can they not blow away black sand?
[Section Two: Requesting an Explanation] Below, the explanation is now provided in two parts. First, the Sūtra clarifies the colors of the winds.
The *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* states: "Black winds swirl in waves. The *Ratnaketu-parājitadhvaja-sūtra* (Renwang bore) mentions six types of colored winds: black, red, blue, and so forth.
Heaven and earth are fire; they receive the *yin* [essence] and manifest the five winds. The *Āgama* also speaks of "black winds.
When these two winds are added to the wind below, the black terror is extreme;
that is, when the winds are augmented by black, the terror is most intense.
III. The Rākṣasas Suffering Below.
The rākṣasa is a man-eating ghost; if human corpses become putrid, it can employ incantations to nourish them so they remain fresh. Furthermore, there are ghosts that devour vital essence (*ojas*);
within the human heart, there are seven drops of sweet water which nourish the spirit. The ghost devours one drop at a time.
Three drops cause a headache; seven drops cause fainting; at ten drops, death occurs immediately. [Commentary]:
As for the rākṣasa demons, they were originally under the jurisdiction of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King.
There are two classes: the first is called yakṣas, the swift-moving demons; the second is called rākṣasas, the man-eating demons. They are found everywhere. However...

The lands where they originally resided were across the sea; some people drifted there by chance, while others were spirits who came here to harass humans—all because of the connection of past evil causes.
(4) From "One person" below, the capacity [of the recipient] is clarified.
One person calls out the name.
○ Fifth, the response of the enlightened ones:
when others are all liberated, those who share in the common experience of sorrow, joy, misfortune, or prosperity—though they do not chant together with their mouths—assist with their hearts.
Because they seek merit, both obtain salvation equally. However, if they subsequently encounter bandits, those who chant in unison will prevail;
on land, the mind is often divided and cannot be unified, so it is essential to call out the name together to ensure harmony, just as it is with the danger of water.
II. The second section, "For what purpose," concludes the names.

For what purpose does he conclude the name of Avalokiteśvara here? This is precisely a case of designating the name based on a single individual, yet it relies upon the inclusion of his followers to clarify that the power of compassion is extensively pervasive and that protection is impartial; thus, it reveals the true meaning of the name "Avalokiteśvara."
II. Regarding the second [section], the verification through actual events:

The *Yingyan zhuan* (Traditions of Miraculous Responses) states that more than one hundred people from foreign lands were sailing across the sea from Siṃhala Island toward Funan when they suddenly encountered a violent wind and fell into a land of ghosts.
The ghosts were about to devour the entire ship, and the multitude was terrified.
Among those who invoke Avalokiteśvara, there was once a śramaṇa of the Hīnayāna who did not believe in Avalokiteśvara and refused to call upon his name.
When a ghost seized this śramaṇa, he was driven into a state of panic and learned to invoke the name; thus, he too was delivered and escaped.
III. Explanation through the Three Contemplations (Sanguan). Part 1: Clarifying that the meaning of "wind" (feng) is not limited.
Second, as for the explanation through contemplation: it clarifies that "wind" is not merely the wind within the world-system;

the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the fierce winds of resentment blow upon the fire of the sinful mind, constantly causing it to blaze, and blow upon the merchants of formative action (*saṃskāra*), causing them to fall into evil [destinies].
One loses the human path, the treasures of human goodness, and the untainted wealth of the noble ones.

[Commentary] Within the world, there are winds that are the result of karmic retribution; "winds" refers to dark karma. Thus, from the loss of the human path and the treasures of goodness, all are the winds of evil karma.
The loss of the untainted wealth is the wind of affliction (*kleśa*). Below this, the fifth section further clarifies this.

Because it is difficult to fully elucidate the meaning of the "three obstacles" (trivibandha) and "evil ghosts" (pāpaka-preta), I shall now, in the context of contemplative practice, briefly demonstrate them according to the principle of "difficulties arising from wind.
This serves as the model for clarifying the distinct and perfect contemplations within the six types [of samādhi], which are the very pattern for all objects of contemplation.
II. Explaining the Wind from Below, which Penetrates the Three Obstructions. Part One: The Retribution. Section One: Encountering Suffering.
Subsection One: Ascending to the Third Dhyāna.
From the hells up to the Third Dhyāna, there are all difficulties caused by the winds of retribution.

2. Just as the Saṃgha [descends] to the lowest realms, pervading all destinies—just as the *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* clarifies the various forms and appearances in the hells: being submerged and destroyed by swift winds and fierce waves;

being devoured in the realm of hungry ghosts, where they are gnawed by spirits; and in the animal realm, being scattered like crumbling stones by cold winds that pierce the bones. Flying [as birds], etc.
As for the species that move on land, their nests overturned and eggs destroyed—how could one ever finish recounting it? The asuras also face the calamity of wind;
when the wind disaster arises, the various mountains collide and strike one another, reaching up to the palaces of the third dhyāna heaven, shattering them into fine dust.
[Commentary: The bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita was an eminent teacher of the four Āgamas for the assembly.

Five hundred merchants who had gone to sea to gather treasures came to the World-Honored One and requested that this bhikṣu preach the Dharma to them on board their ship. The Buddha, knowing it would be beneficial, granted the request and sent him away.
When the ship returned to shore, he disembarked and traveled on land, staying overnight beneath a tree. The merchants set out early the next morning.
The monk Vismṛtāhvāna (Forgetful) lost his companions thereupon and traveled alone through the mountain forests. There he saw a monastery where monks resided;
whatever food and drink, dwellings, heated rooms, gardens, fields, or articles of enjoyment were there, they were all instruments of suffering.
Day and night, he endured more than a hundred varieties of such suffering. Saṃgharakṣita asked him:
Therefore, they all replied, "You should return and ask the Buddha; he will know for himself. Once they had reached the Buddha’s presence, they related in detail what they had seen.

The Buddha answered them all, explaining that these were monks who had violated the various prohibitions, destroyed the permanent assets of the Sangha, and misappropriated communal property, and were consequently undergoing the sufferings of hell upon that mountain in the sea.
Students who examine this account should take it as sufficient cause for self-reproach.
Second, the following section clarifies the response to the capacity [of sentient beings].
At this time, who is able to provide salvation? One should single-mindedly invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;
through the power of his sovereign samādhi, he employs immeasurable skillful means—whether shielding with his hand or inhaling with his mouth—to enable them to attain liberation.
Liberation.
○ Second, clarifying the inferior karmic actions of the lower realms: first, encountering calamities;

second, clarifying that if one practices various wholesome deeds, yet the winds of evil karma blow away the vessel of the five precepts and ten wholesome paths, one falls into the three [evil realms].
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that in the realm of ghosts and the sphere of craving views (*tṛṣṇādṛṣṭi*), rākṣasī women devour every son they give birth to;
once their sons have been consumed, they further devour their husbands.

[Commentary] Regarding the three miserable realms (*durgati*), they pertain to the fruit; regarding craving and views, they pertain to the cause. Both arise due to past karma, causing one to fall into the three miserable realms through craving and views.
A mind of greed is like a rākṣasī woman; violating the precepts and meditative goodness is like losing the reward of human or celestial rebirth, just as she devours her own son or her husband.
II. The necessity of responding to those of inferior capacity.
It is necessary to invoke Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, for by the power of his compassion, he can bring about liberation. III.
Third, clarifying the afflictions of those of inferior capacity. Part one: clarifying the capacity. 1. Śrāvakas.

Next, it is explained that when followers of the Two Vehicles gather the treasures of the noble wealth, their ship of wisdom and practice is blown by the winds of affliction and driven into the realm of views and craving,
where they are harmed by the rākṣasas of views and craving. If they can invoke Avalokiteśvara,
they will be liberated from the two wheels of views and craving and forever escape the black karma of the twenty-five states of existence.

[Commentary]: The noble wealth (*ārya-dhana*) does not exceed seven types: first, hearing; second, faith; third, precepts; fourth, concentration; fifth, diligence; sixth, relinquishment; and seventh, shame and dread.
Regarding the practice of wisdom, there are the analytical contemplations on impermanence; regarding the practice of conduct, there are the two types of practice such as impurity and loving-kindness.

These two types of practice refer to what is cultivated during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), while the seven types of wealth refer to what is attained during the stage of a noble one (*ārya*).
Next, the second section clarifies the various stages below.

It further elucidates how the Pratyekabuddhas, through the practice of the six pāramitās—both in their general and specific aspects, and in their transformational and perfect modes—enter the sea of afflictions to gather the jewel of *sarvajñatā*.
Yet they are buffeted by the violent winds of the eight inversions, causing their vessel of conditioned formations to drift and fall into the ghost-realm of the two extremes.

By correctly contemplating the essence of the mind and realizing that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, one enters into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and thereby attains liberation.
As for the meaning of "ghost" (*preta*), it is not explained again here because it has already been integrated with the preceding and subsequent chapters.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "winds of the eight inversions": for those who enter the contemplation of emptiness through the distinct and perfect [teachings] of the Pratyekabuddhas and the Six Pāramitās, taking the "permanent" and so forth as inversions;

and for those who transform the provisional and the middle [realms], taking the "impermanent" and so forth as inversions—by employing right contemplation with a single mind to invoke Avalokiteśvara, one immediately emerges from the realm of the evil ghosts of the two extremes and is able to reach the precious island of the Middle Way. As for the ghosts...

Regarding the thematic connection between the preceding and following chapters: the former refers to this chapter’s topical commentary on the matter of phenomena (*dharma*), while the latter refers to the fifth chapter, "The Objections of the Ghosts.
2. From "The Dharma-realm" onwards, it clarifies the response [to the objections]. This has two parts: first, a general demonstration of the compassion of the two contemplations.
That the winds of the Dharma-realm respond perfectly and simultaneously to immeasurable difficulties is entirely due to the permeation of the distinct and perfect [teachings] of compassion.
[Commentary]: Although the distinct [teaching] involves gradual cultivation, its fruit is capable of perfect response.

II. Specifically clarifying the two types of samādhi—gradual and sudden—for those below the stage of the Bodhisattva. First, the gradual approach. A. At the time of cultivation, one makes vows in accordance with one's practice.

When a Bodhisattva originally cultivates specific contemplations and perceives the wind within phenomena, they immediately give rise to compassion and cultivate the precepts and meditative concentration (*śīla-samādhi*). Upon seeing evil...
The karma-winds immediately arise; when practicing the three contemplations with compassion at every stage, one practices compassion at every moment.
○ Second, "Now entering" and below clarifies that at the time of realization, one responds to difficulties as they arise.
Now, by entering the *Vāyu-tattva-rāja-samādhi*, one uses phenomenal compassion (*vastu-karuṇā*) to rescue the winds of karmic retribution through the precepts.

Through the concentration of compassion that rescues from the winds of evil karma, and through the three contemplations of compassion that rescue from the winds of affliction, one is able to extricate others from calamities in ten ways.
Second, regarding the sudden [attainment] below, there are two parts; first, at the time of cultivation, the three truths are perfectly interfused.
If one practices this as a circular contemplation regarding the correspondence between the capacity and the response, one should simply contemplate the gateway of the letter *vā*;
it fully illuminates the ten dharma-realms and the three truths, which are perfectly manifest, penetrating without obstruction, and universally covered by great compassion.
[Commentary] Regarding the "gate of the letter V" (*vā*), as explained in the *Pínguānyīn shū* (Commentary on the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara) in the section on the six characters:

the six realms of existence and so forth are taken as the gates of the six characters because the essence of the six realms is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and because they can lead one through to the true reality (*tattva*), they are called "gates.
Now, taking the letter V as a gate, its meaning is likewise so. A "letter" (*akṣara*) is a term used to summon or designate a phenomenon.
II. If one distinguishes the application during the momentary differentiation, and explains the King Samādhi in detail:

one employs seventeen samādhis to rescue the winds of karmic retribution, twenty-four samādhis to rescue the winds of cultivating causes, and twenty-five samādhis to rescue the common and distinct [paths] of the two vehicles.

The Perfect Teaching rescues those entering emptiness from the winds of affliction by means of the twenty-five samādhis; it rescues those of the Separate Teaching entering the provisional from the winds of ignorance by means of the twenty-five samādhis;
and it rescues those of the Perfect Teaching entering the Middle Way from the winds of ignorance by means of the twenty-five samādhis.
The transformation of the body through birth-and-death is thus understood. In this way, all throughout the Dharma-realm are universally rescued, and at one and the same time, all attain liberation.
IV. The Peril of Weapons and Sticks (Śastra-daṇḍa-vighna). Part 1: Listing the Sections.

Regarding the fourth [section], the elucidation of the peril of weapons and sticks, it is also divided into three: first, the topical commentary (*pāṭha*); second, the application of scriptural evidence (*sūtra-pramāṇa*); and third, the interpretive explanation through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
II. Explanation of the Text A. Initial Analysis of the Sūtra B.
Application of the Text (in three parts): 1. Encountering calamity is itself suffering; 2. Invoking the name is itself goodness; 3. The response.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who, when about to be harmed, calls upon the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
the swords and staves held by their assailants will immediately break into pieces, and they shall obtain liberation.
II. Explanation of the Meaning (in three parts): A. First, encountering the calamity; B. Second, invoking the name; C. Third, "Now, as for... and below, receiving the response. 1.
The first part [C] explains according to the text:

"Now, as for the swords and staves being broken into pieces" clarifies that whenever a person grasps a weapon to kill, it breaks into one piece at a time, and as each piece comes forth, it is destroyed.
The more it is severed, the more its great power is revealed.
II. Questioning and analyzing the preceding [section] in response, part one: the question.
Question: Why do water and fire not cause [the other] to be extinguished a second time?
II. The Response. [The opponent] replies:

"If the swords and staves were broken, they would have to be brought back again to further manifest the power of the Sage. Since there is no one to bring them back after the fire and water have extinguished them, what could be manifested by that extinction?
