Second, to clarify the distinctions according to individual capacities:
if one were to explain them analytically, the thirteen samādhis save the ghosts of worldly affairs; the twenty-four samādhis save the ghosts of evil karma;
and the twenty-five samādhis save the ghosts of those of the Two Vehicles who have entered emptiness through the Shared, Distinct, and Complete teachings, and so forth.
Upon entering the Middle Way, all are simultaneously and entirely rendered incapable of causing harm.

[Commentary: Since the spirits who serve ghosts are able to afflict Śakra, the gods dwelling on earth, the four continents, and the four realms of existence experience the power of the ten kinds of kingly samādhis;
the remaining meanings are the same as before.
○ VI. The Objection Concerning Shackles and Locks (Śṛṅkhalābandhana-vipratipatti). Part One: Listing the Sections.

The sixth objection concerning shackles and locks also consists of three parts: (1) Adhering to the Text (pāṭha-anusāra), (2) Correlating with Scriptural Authority (pramāṇa-saṃvāda), and (3) Exegesis through Contemplation (vipaśyanā-vyākhyāna).
○ Part Two: Detailed Explanation. Three sections. First, adhering to the text. Part One: Segmenting the Sūtra.
The post is divided into four parts: first, whether one has committed a crime or not; second, encountering calamity; third, invoking the name; and fourth, the response.

Furthermore, if there is anyone—whether guilty or innocent—who is bound and fettered by shackles, manacles, stocks, or chains, and invokes the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, all these bonds shall be severed and destroyed, and they will immediately attain liberation.
II. Explaining the Meaning of "The Superior Overlooking the Inferior. Section Four: First, the specification of the offense.
When the superior overlooks [the crime] and the victim is about to suffer harm, this is definitively categorized as a death sentence. This clarifies whether there is an offense or not;

it may be that the investigation has not yet been finalized, or it may be that a judgment of penal servitude or exile can be rendered. Whether the judgment has been rendered or not, both cases involve confinement and restraint. This clarifies the Sage’s [teaching].
The mind and its associates fundamentally seek to rescue those held in captivity, regardless of whether they are guilty or innocent.
Second, suffering misfortune while under the hand [of the authorities]:

that which is on the hands is called *xiǔ* (handcuffs), that which is on the feet is called *xiè* (fetters), that which is around the neck is called *jiā* (a wooden collar), and that which binds the entire body is called *suǒ* (shackles). These constitute three.

"Wood" and "iron" are names for binding; "binding" refers to the act of tying, while "sealing" refers to the sealing of a container. While being bound does not necessarily entail being sealed, being sealed inevitably entails being bound.
When one is both bound and sealed, the resulting anxiety and fear are profound.
○ Third, when a bird dies, it utters its name;
when a bird dies, its cry is mournful, and when a person dies, their words are good. If one can invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara...
[Commentary] Zengzi said: "When a bird is about to die, its cry is mournful; when a person is about to die, their words..."
Excellent.
○ Fourth, Receiving the Response:
The double gates open of their own accord, and the iron and wood are shattered and destroyed.
II. Regarding the facts.
Next, to cite a factual testimony as proof, the *Yingyan zhuan* (Records of Miraculous Responses) states: "Hu of Shanyang was imprisoned and was to be executed.
For three days and three nights, his mind never ceased its focus; consequently, he saw Guanyin emitting light that shone upon him, whereby his shackles fell off and the gates opened."
He opened his eyes and followed the light for twenty *li* until the radiance finally faded. Zhang Chang was serving as the Chief Secretary to Prince Qiao;

when both the Prince and Chang were imprisoned in the Court of Judicial Review, he recited the sutras one thousand times, whereupon the shackles broke apart inch by inch and they were released before long.
(The account of Minister of Works Xu continues...)

III. Explanation by means of the Three Contemplations (Sanguan) regarding the Two [Categories]: First, the Direct Clarification of Shackles and Locks; Second, the Ripening of Karmic Retribution. First, the Clarification of Difficulties:

Regarding the explanation by means of the Three Contemplations, the essence of the hells is that of a prison; ghosts and animals likewise have cages and fetters; even the asuras are bound by the five shackles.
As for those in the northern regions and the heavens who possess sovereignty, one might think they should be free from such hardships. Having addressed this, [the following follows].
There is still no escape from the hardships of the dark realms.
[Record: The circumstances of these matters pertain exclusively to the four destinies and the three continents.
Second, the section beginning with "If one can" clarifies the resulting retribution.
If one can recite the name, all [karmic obstacles] shall be severed and destroyed.
Second, the secondary explanation of the evil karma of the lower realms: first, explaining the difficulty;
second, explaining the cultivation of causes. Evil karma is precisely what is called shackles and fetters; although various karmas possess power, they do not pursue one who does not follow them.
Because an agent who has committed an action will never lose its fruit, it is called an "indestructible dharma" (*avipraṇāśa-dharma*), like a promissory note.
If a person cultivates various virtues but they are obscured by evil karma—just as a great mountain casts a shadow that covers the mind—the virtues are destroyed and further evil karma is increased.
This evil karma then brings about the bondage of its fruit, from which there is no way of escape.
Second, regarding the section "If one wishes" and below, this clarifies the response [to suffering].
If one wishes to be liberated from these karmic actions, one may seek urgent relief at the time of the cause by invoking Avalokiteśvara, which can cause the three evil karmas to be destroyed.
Third, the scripture cited below:
Thus the scripture says, "Wife and children are taken as shackles; wealth and property are taken as a prison; the laws of the king are taken as the prison register.
These obstruct the traveler so that they cannot practice the Way. Viewed in terms of the present, these are bonds of karmic retribution; viewed in terms of the future..."
"Depart from this karma.

[Commentary: Regarding those detained by the Minister of Justice (*tingwei*), there may be a time for release; however, as for wives, children, and wealth, there is no day of liberation from their bondage.
As for "hopes for the present," etc., even one's current wife, children, and wealth are both karma and retribution (*vipāka*). Why? Because if they...

What is manifested in the present is called "retribution" (*vipāka*); what is spoken of in relation to the past is called "karma" (*karman*). One should know that all obstacles to the wholesome are due to past evils.

These past evils may have already matured into retribution, in which case they act as obstacles by attaching themselves to that retribution—such as one's current wife, children, and the environment of dependent retribution (*upabhoga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
If they have not yet matured into retribution, they currently exist within the path of karma (*karmapatha*) and likewise possess their own [obstructive power].
Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that one's wife and others will act as obstacles to the cultivation of goodness;

rather, if they have together cultivated roots of virtue in past lives, they can now serve as auxiliary conditions for the path to awakening. For example, King Subhavyūha, through the influence of his wife and children, beheld the Buddha and attained enlightenment.
We see in the present day people whose wives and children exhort them toward goodness, and who, having accumulated wealth, are able to practice generosity—whereas previously they followed after evil.

The wife and others who are experienced as a result of causes are called "fetters" and "prisons. If one returns to Avalokiteśvara, then both those karmic retributions already completed and those not yet completed—all such evils—will cease.

○ Third, the explanation of the secondary afflictions has two parts: first, explaining the capacity [of the practitioner]; second, first, applying it to the Śrāvakas; second, first, applying it to... [text fragment].
Brief Explanation of the Two [Points]: First, the clarification of the objection;
second, the clarification regarding the śrāvakas. All ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in the first three fruits are guilty, whereas the arhat is without fault.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The mahānāgas, whether guilty or without fault, are all together within the prison of the triple world. Five.

Bound by the ropes of the aggregates (*skandha*), constrained by the seal of the three marks of impermanence, and sealed by the provisional and ultimate truths, the delusions of the upper [level] regarding view are called shackles;
the delusions of the upper [level] regarding meditation and wisdom are called fetters; the delusions of the middle path are called stocks; and the delusions of the dharma-body are called chains.
Bound by such things, the practitioner is unable to attain liberation.

[Commentary]: Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in the first three fruits (*phala*) who still possess all the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), and whose afflictions of thought are not yet exhausted, are all termed "guilty" (*sāparādha*).

An Arhat whose afflictions of thought are exhausted is termed "guiltless" (*niraparādha*). Since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* identifies those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) as "Great Dragons," it says "mahānāga.
The remaining afflictions of one in training are called "guilty," while their total eradication by one beyond training is called [guiltless].

Those who are without fault, yet are neither entirely free from remainder, are said to be "together in prison. Since they already possess a resultant body, how could they escape the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the three marks (*tri-lakṣaṇa*)?

This is what is meant by being "bound and fettered. Regarding the provisional and the ultimate: this refers to the demonstration of those with faults. To obstruct the two wisdoms (*dvi-jñāna*) is called "handcuffs" (*nigaḍa*);
to hinder the two practices (*dvi-caryā*) from advancing is called "shackles" (*śṛṅkhalā*). The "small" [fetters] consist of [the views of] annihilationism and eternalism (*uccheda-śāśvata*).

The shackles of the Middle Way can obstruct the five aggregates; as fetters for the Dharma-body, they are specifically termed "handcuffs" and so forth in relation to what they obstruct—namely, the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
Second, following the title, the response is explained.
If one invokes the name and maintains mindfulness, one will certainly receive spiritual response: if fixed wisdom and adaptive wisdom arise, it is as if the shackles are severed;

if provisional and ultimate truths are revealed, it is as if the cangues are severed; if ignorance is destroyed, it is as if the collar is severed; if the Dharma-body manifests, it is as if the fetters are severed;
if one enters Nirvana without remainder, it is as if the bonds are severed; to be exempt from the three marks is to escape the search; to emerge from the triple world is to leave the prison.
[Commentary] Second, the section beginning with "This further... clarifies the commonality with the Mahāyāna.
This, in turn, possesses both common and specific meanings.

[Commentary] If one discusses the fetters of common delusions (*sāmānya-kleśa*), then the shackles and manacles refer to those of the *Hīnayāna* (Āgama) and *Pratyekabuddha* (Sautrāntika) vehicles; if one explains the shackles in terms of specific delusions (*viśeṣa-kleśa*), [the meaning differs].
The "Xie" and others refer to those of the Separate (Bian) and Perfect (Yuan) vehicles.
Second, it explains the subsequent examples for the various stages.
Next, it clarifies that the practice of the Six Paramitas by Pratyekabuddhas encompasses both the Separate and the Perfect.
Second, regarding the section below on "manifesting responsiveness":

even the shackles and fetters are still the substance of the earth; the meaning of the compassionate and universal responsiveness arising from the fundamental contemplation of the Distinct and Perfect Vehicles is no different from what was explained previously.

[Commentary] Regarding the causes, the gradual and sudden aspects of compassion, and regarding the fruit, the perfect and universal aspects of both bestowing [benefits] and removing [suffering], are all as explained above.
Second, from "If three" onwards, it concurrently clarifies both emptiness and consciousness. First, "universally responding" refers back to what was previously stated.

If the three thousandfold great chiliocosm represents the element of space (*ākāśa-dhātu*), and kings, thieves, ghosts, and the like represent the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*), then discussing these ten stages universally corresponds to what was previously stated.

Second, regarding the fundamental contemplation of the lower [stages], there are now two parts: first, the gradual; second, the fundamental contemplation of compassion. First, the fundamental contemplation of compassion. Second... [text continues].
First, the preliminary contemplation has been shown.

Now, regarding the fundamental contemplation, it shall be explained: when a bodhisattva perceives sentient beings, they realize that the fruit and retribution of existence are produced by emptiness-consciousness (*śūnyatā-vijñāna*).
Yet, as they cultivate various virtues, they see that the karma of this emptiness-consciousness can also destroy those virtues. Thus one should contemplate.
Within emptiness and consciousness, there are the obstacles of the three truths and the principles of the three truths;
thus, at every stage, one gives rise to compassion—desiring to extract the suffering of sentient beings through pity, and desiring to bestow happiness upon sentient beings through loving-kindness.

[Commentary] All afflictions are produced by consciousness; consciousness is most difficult to empty. Although it is not inherently difficult, because it brings about what is difficult, emptiness is also called "difficult emptiness" (*duḥkha-śūnyatā*).
As for emptiness being an action, it is also an action because, due to the presence of internal space within the body, one is able to move and perform karmic deeds.
External space is likewise so. As for emptiness being a delusion, it refers to confusion regarding objects. As for emptiness being awakening, it refers to clarity regarding objects.
Whether all phenomena are obstacles or principles, whether all phenomena are erroneous or correct, one should give rise to vows at every stage to extract [beings] from them.
Second, "Therefore, it is pure" and below, citing scriptures as proof.

Therefore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "When a bodhisattva contemplates that the four great elements, the element of space, and the element of consciousness are all empty and void, there are no four great elements, no space, and no consciousness;
this is called entering the gate of non-dual dharmas."
[Commentary] In the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality," the Bodhisattva Lakṣaṇa said: "To regard the four kinds of elements as distinct from the nature of space is duality.
The four kinds of natures are themselves the nature of space, for just as the prior limit and the posterior limit are empty, so too is the middle limit empty.
If one can know all such natures in this way, this is entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Since it has been said:
The four kinds of nature are themselves the nature of emptiness; this clarifies that emptiness is revealed through its very nature. This middle way is the principle within emptiness.

Because this middle way does not bifurcate into two regarding phenomena, those [four] are non-dual in terms of their fivefold nature. Now, when clarifying the six kinds, how could they not be identical to that nature?
Thus, by capturing the intent of the sutra, the addition of the "consciousness-element" further manifests non-duality. If it were merely emptiness and consciousness...
If it were not the Middle Way, what would serve as the essence of the King Samādhi?
Second, regarding the fulfillment of the vow to descend and respond for the sake of those on the lower vehicles, there are two parts: first, showing the manifestation;
the King Samādhi is able to pervade the ten dharma-realms and manifest responses through compassionate deeds to rescue beings from their karmic retributions.

It is difficult for emptiness and consciousness to cultivate goodness and compassion to save one from evil karma; it is difficult for emptiness and consciousness to employ the three contemplations and compassion to save one from afflictions.
Because emptiness and consciousness are so difficult [to master], we know that Avalokiteśvara has attained mastery within the dharma-gate of emptiness and consciousness.
II. Quotations from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
In the thirty-ninth fascicle of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, it is stated that the Bhikṣu Susthita performs great Buddha-activities within empty space.
[Commentary] Seeing the true mark of emptiness enables one to establish various deeds within empty space to benefit all sentient beings.
II. Second, regarding the two methods of sudden and gradual practice: first, the perfect cultivation of emptiness and consciousness.

If one practices the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*), observing that the causes, conditions, nature, characteristics, beginning, end, and ultimate reality of emptiness are equal, then all ten dharma realms will entirely enter the gate of emptiness, and consciousness is likewise so.

[Commentary]: Among the various methods for contemplating phenomena, most emphasize the mind and consciousness because they are proximate and essential; furthermore, since beginners find them easy to grasp, there are differences in the faculties of people.

Thus, some may benefit by contemplating external objects. Within the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), sentient beings of the lower realms are mostly attached to external things, so they are instructed to withdraw from objects and contemplate the internal mind. Sentient beings of the upper realms, however, are mostly attached to the internal mind.

Therefore, one is caused to contemplate form so as to overcome internal attachment; now, contemplating the empty elements (*ākāśa-dhātu*) is likewise a category of form—being but a single form—because there is no phenomenon outside of emptiness.
Thus, all ten realms entirely enter the gate of emptiness. Since emptiness is the three truths (*tri-satya*), all phenomena are identical with the three truths.
The three truths, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and non-arising (*anutpāda*) encompass all things.
Second, arising non-inferior compassion that universally responds:
by giving rise to unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*) that permeates all sentient beings, whenever there is a capacity within the ten dharma realms,
all may simultaneously attain liberation.

The topical outline of the scripture consists of four sections based on the text: first, identifying the point of difficulty; second, identifying the person who encounters the difficulty; third, clarifying that there is an opportunity [for salvation]; and fourth, clarifying the appropriate response.
If the trichiliocosm were filled with hostile bandits.
[Section Two: Explaining the Meaning of the Difficult Places. Part One: Indicating the Difficult Places. First, clarifying the location.
Regarding "difficult places," first one clarifies the location, which is the trichiliocosm.
○ Second, explaining the difficulty of being filled. First, regarding the explanation of "being filled":
next, the "difficulty of being filled" refers to the phrase "the enemy bandits fill the midst," which is a hypothetical expression.
That the country is vast and the bandits are many, yet the power of the Sage can save them, demonstrates the ultimate nature of his merit.
Second, regarding "enemies" (*vairin*), this explains the "enemies who are thieves.
An enemy is a grave danger; a thief originally targets wealth, while an enemy originally robs one's life. Now, when an enemy acts as a thief, they surely plot against both wealth and life.
Thus, those who caused bloodshed in the past are called "enemies," while those who seize wealth in the present are called "thieves. It is like this.
If he can even protect those who are surrounded by hostile bandits filling the great trichiliocosm, how could he not save those whose afflictions are slight?
Part Two: Identifying the persons who encounter calamities; Section One: Presenting four meanings.
Second, regarding the designation of the person who encounters the calamity, this refers to the caravan leader. This is further divided into four aspects: first, the leader; second, having followers;
third, carrying treasures; and fourth, traversing dangerous paths.
There was a caravan leader who, taking various merchants with him, carried heavy treasures as they passed through a perilous road.
II. Regarding the second term, "merchant" (*śreṣṭhin*), there follows an explanation of its four meanings. First, the explanation of the "merchant leader":

"Merchant" (*śreṣṭhin*) is glossed as "measuring. This person possesses discerning consciousness regarding value and is skilled in understanding financial profit; because he is capable of deliberating on what is appropriate, he is fit to be the leader of merchants.
○ Second, "Since there are already... explains the merchants.
Since there is already a caravan leader, there are those who lead the various merchants.
○ Third, "Since they have traveled far... explains the precious treasures.
Since they have traveled through dangerous and distant regions, the goods they carry must necessarily be rare commodities; hence the term "precious treasures.
[Commentary] By noting the large number of people and the great distance of the road, the preciousness of the goods they carry is made manifest.
○ Fourth, the perilous road. To explain the perilous road below:
a "perilous road" may refer to a place that is desolate and remote, or narrow and confined;
or it may refer to a place where one encounters enemies or bandits making a sudden sortie.
[Commentary] The term "perilous" (*kian*) is explained through two matters: the location and the person. III.
Regarding the "three capacities" (*san-ki*), the following clarifies that there are those with capacity. Part one: showing the four meanings of the sutra.
Capacity also has four aspects: first, a single person’s consolation; second, exhorting the recitation of the name; third, praising his virtues; fourth, the assembly.
All the people together raised their voices, and one among them proclaimed: "Good sons, do not be afraid!
You should all with one mind invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; this Bodhisattva is able to bestow fearlessness upon all beings."
"Jīva, if you all invoke my name, you shall be liberated from these hostile bandits.
When the merchants heard this, they all raised their voices together and said, "Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva! Because they invoked his name, they were immediately liberated.

II. The second section provides a general explanation of the four meanings. This is divided into two parts: first, clarifying how the preceding three serve as aids for progress; second, the actual explanation.
Regarding the first part, it clarifies why the three [practices] are established.
As for "providing comfort," it is to quell their fear. As for "encouraging the recitation of the name," it is to establish the superior [practice].
The reason why [the Buddha] sighed in admiration of his virtue was to encourage him to steady his resolve.
[Commentary]: To single-mindedly recite the name is the supreme strategy; there is nothing superior to this. Knowing that one’s virtue can be relied upon, one’s resolve becomes firm.

Regarding the proof by means of specific events, the *Yingyan zhuan* (Account of Manifestations) states that in the second year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, Huida [was at] Beilong...
At that time, while digging for licorice roots, the Qiang people were starving and captured people to eat them. Da was seized by the Qiang and confined within their stockades;
they selected the fattest individuals to eat first. When most of the others had been consumed, it was Da’s turn along with a small child, who were slated to be eaten the following day.
Da recited the name [of the Buddha] and chanted the sutras with focused single-mindedness throughout the entire night, still hoping for a single sign of response.
At dawn, the Qiang came to seize him; suddenly, a tiger burst forth from the grass, roaring, whereupon the Qiang scattered and fled.
The tiger then bit through the palisade, making a hole, and departed. Da led the child away and defected, thus escaping.
Later, when Pei Anqi returned from the barbarians and traveled south toward the riverbank, he was unable to cross; looking back, he saw the pursuing cavalry.
Later, when he was on the verge of death after a mere moment had passed, he invoked Avalokiteśvara.

He saw a white wolf that calmly stood up, leaped across, and threw him onto the southern bank; thus he immediately lost the wolf. The pursuing riders remained together on the northern bank, gazing at him and lamenting boundlessly.

II. General Designation and Subsequent Explanation of the Sūtra’s Meaning. Part III: First, explaining the three poisons based on the sūtras and śāstras.
A. General Explanation. 1. Clarifying the single and multiple designations.
They are generally termed "poisons" (*viṣa*) because they afflict the practitioner, being analogous to poison; however, their names may be used either singly or in combination.
[Commentary]: It is asked: "Greed, hatred, and delusion—these three are single [terms]. Why are they now listed as compounds? Therefore, it says: "lustful desire, malice, and folly.
The *Daben shu* (Great Commentary) states: "To love oneself is 'desire' (*yù*); to love others is 'lustful desire' (*yínyù*). To be angry with oneself is 'resentment' (*èi*);
to be angry with others is 'malice' (*chēn*). To be deluded about oneself is 'folly' (*yú*); to be deluded about others is 'delusion' (*chí*)."
II. Regarding the second section, "There are some people," which clarifies the degree [of their practice], it is first explained that others hold there to be few.
Some interpret this as follows: those with much of the three poisons do not recognize that [the Bodhisattva] is their refuge, and therefore do not seek Avalokiteśvara;
those who have little [of the three poisons] recollect the virtue of Avalokiteśvara’s pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and thus are able to evoke his response.

Regarding the second point, "The intention is as follows" and below, this clarifies that the two [previous] positions are insufficient; first, it establishes that the limited view contradicts the sūtra.
The intention is that this interpretation deviates from the text, for the text states: "If there are sentient beings who have much lustful desire, they immediately attain liberation.
How can this be in direct contradiction with the sūtra?
Second, "Now I clarify" and below explains that many [instances] can bring about the result.
Here, it clarifies that those with a predominance of the three poisons are able to call upon Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, who possesses the power to enable them to attain liberation;
how much more so for those with fewer [afflictions]. This is an illustration of the few by means of the many.
[Commentary]: The degree of poison depends on the weight of one's habitual practice; its removal is sought through progress and does not depend on whether a capacity exists.

Those without such capacity fail to seek liberation regardless of whether the poison is great or small. Conversely, those with such capacity are able to seek liberation from both great and small amounts of poison.

The ancients did not understand that by clinging to the "great" they failed to seek it out; today we clearly know that if one can maintain mindfulness, one may be liberated even if the poison is abundant.

The *Mahā-śāstra* Explains Past Causes. The *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"Women, due to being defiled by the precepts and slandering the Dharma, [suffer] the remaining retribution."

[Commentary] The intent is the same as this sutra: the sin of slandering the sutras leads one through all the evil realms; even if one attains a human body, lust will be so rampant that one makes no distinction between humans and beasts.
If one does not seek liberation, one will sink back into the miserable destinies with no prospect of release.
Second, the faults and calamities resulting from failing to discern inferior matters in the present are explained:
by failing to discern [the danger of] birds and beasts, one does not avoid the perils of high walls and deep moats;

by disregarding reputation and virtuous conduct, one brings ruin upon the family, the state, and the clan, destroying the ancestral line and extending the disaster to one's own person—just as the calamity of Śūrpaka extended to his entire kingdom.
It was like the Zhou dynasty’s defeat at the hands of Bao Xi.
[Commentary] The story of Śūrpaka is briefly as recorded in the *Xuánjì*. Bao Xi was a woman from the state of Bao.
King You of Zhou attacked Bao, and the people of Bao presented Xi to the king; he became utterly infatuated with her. Initially, King You [conferred titles] upon the feudal lords...
Whenever there was an imminent threat of invasion, he would strike the drums and raise the beacon fires, and the feudal lords would come to his aid.

However, when he became infatuated with Bao Si, Bao Si did not laugh; the King desired her to laugh, so he struck the drums and raised the beacon fires, causing all the feudal lords to arrive, yet there was no invasion, and Si then laughed.
Furthermore, she delighted in hearing the sound of tearing silk; he tore silk to satisfy her whim. This continued until the time of Shen Hou.

Accompanied by the Qunong troops, they arrived and beat their drums and raised the beacon fires; the feudal lords, believing as before that they were being deceived, did not come again, and consequently suffered defeat.

For example, when a person encounters calamity and is due to face royal punishment, yet an evil person assists them in committing further wickedness—such as by employing harmful insects or spirits—the one who so assists is like the royal punishment;
this is the characteristic of having much desire (*bahukāmatā*). Conversely, if one acts otherwise, it is called the characteristic of having little [desire].

III. Three Questions on Detachment: Clarifying Constant Mindfulness through Question and Answer. Part One: An Objection Concerning Mindfulness Not Being Free from Defilements.
Question: To detach from afflictions one requires wisdom; how can mere mindfulness possibly achieve detachment?
II. Second, the answer to the Sūtra: Explaining mindfulness as being identical to wisdom. This section has two parts: first, a brief clarification of the virtues of right mindfulness;
second, clarifying the function of wisdom through its identity with mindfulness.

Answering the Sūtra’s statement that "constant mindfulness" is the essence of right mindfulness: it realizes that the nature of afflictions is non-existent, and thus one abides in detachment from greed.
The limit of desire is itself the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); it transcends the four propositions, being without subject or object, and its nature is pure.
Such right mindfulness is not "wisdom"—where else could one find wisdom? This wisdom does not depart from afflictions;
who then could ever depart from them?
[Commentary] Names such as mindfulness (*smṛti*), contemplation (*saṃjñā*), observation (*vipaśyanā*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) possess both faults and virtues, and are either partial or complete.

One must determine the essential nature of these dharmas by means of six propositions. Thus, within the Complete [Teaching], mindfulness breaks through the partial wisdom of the Small Vehicle; the wisdom within the Complete breaks through the partial mindfulness of the Small Vehicle;
the mindfulness of the Small Vehicle cultivates the wisdom within the Complete; and the wisdom of the Small Vehicle cultivates the mindfulness within the Complete.
The mindfulness within the Perfect [Teaching] is precisely the wisdom within the Perfect; the wisdom within the Perfect is precisely the mindfulness within the Perfect.
Only by evaluating the right and wrong of the Dharma through these six phrases can one understand the names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) of all sutras and śāstras.

Because the questioner was ignorant of this, he took what is not mindfulness to be wisdom. Now, since this text on the Perfect explicitly states "constant mindfulness," it is evident that there is no duality of extremes.
The thought that simultaneously negates and illuminates both arising and ceasing is the thought of the Central Mean.

To realize that the nature of afflictions is itself the body of Avalokiteśvara is neither to destroy afflictions nor to establish the Bodhisattva; when destroying and establishing are forgotten, subject and object are severed.

This is what is meant by "constantly mindful of and revering Avalokiteśvara. It is not to be separate from the three poisons while being separate from the three poisons—if there were an Avalokiteśvara to be found...
If, while giving rise to thoughts of conditions, one sees that the three poisons must be extinguished and abandoned, this merely increases the poison rather than abandoning it.
Second, regarding the faults of wisdom as explained through the departure from thought, as in the following passage: [text follows].
If, as you have argued, it is necessary to employ a distinct wisdom to destroy the afflictions, then there must be delusions that can be severed and a wisdom capable of severing them;
it would not be the case that the afflictions cannot be severed while wisdom itself becomes an affliction. How, then, could such [wisdom] be called "the wisdom that severs delusions"?

II. Now, from "In this case" onwards, there is a detailed explanation of the characteristics of cultivating contemplation. This consists of two parts: first, discussing four propositions regarding the separation of forgetting and illumination;

second, discussing four propositions regarding both mindfulness of form and mindfulness of non-form. In this case, right mindfulness does not contemplate by means of form, nor does it contemplate by means of non-form—these are the four propositions.
Likewise, it also contemplates by means of form, and it also contemplates by means of non-form—these are the [other] four propositions.

[Commentary] Since the substance of defilement has been severed by this right mindfulness, forgetting does not obstruct illumination; rather, it is precisely through this illumination that the three truths are realized, and through this forgetting that the three contemplations are attained.
Although four permutations may be posited, only the forgetting of the three contemplations is emphasized, because the "neither-nor" and "both-and" are simply the Middle Way.
Thus, one does not forget the conventional truth by means of the mindfulness of form; nor does one [forget it] by means of non-form, as the case of form serves as an analogy for all phenomena.
Regarding the "forgetting of mindfulness" (念忘), it should be stated as follows: "Not by means of 'neither form nor non-form'—this is the Middle Way of the dual negation;

not by means of 'both form and non-form'—this is the Middle Way of the dual affirmation. If one analyzes these according to the illumination of the three truths, they further constitute four propositions:

"also by means of the mindfulness of form, one illuminates the conventional truth"; "also by means of the mindfulness of non-form, one illuminates the ultimate truth"; and "also by means of... [the third proposition].
One should know that by skillfully forgetting "neither form nor non-form," one illuminates the middle through the simultaneous negation of both;

and by skillfully forgetting "both form and non-form," one illuminates the middle through the simultaneous affirmation of both. One who skillfully forgets the provisional is able to skillfully illuminate the provisional;

one who skillfully forgets emptiness is able to skillfully illuminate emptiness; one who skillfully forgets "neither" is able to illuminate "neither"; and one who skillfully forgets "both" is able to illuminate "both."
Furthermore, there is no need to forget the provisional by means of the empty, nor to forget the empty by means of the provisional; both "neither" and "both" are likewise so.

This is discussed from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching: mindfulness itself is the Dharma-realm, wherein no virtue is not complete. Thus, it is explained through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
To be free and at ease throughout the day while forgetting the four, yet illuminating the four throughout the day—only in this way is one constantly mindful of Avalokiteśvara.
Secondly, there are various fourfold permutations regarding the gradual and sudden [attainments] below that:
either a sequential discourse on non-recollection, or a non-sequential discourse on non-recollection, or a non-sequential discourse on recollection, or a sequential discourse on recollection;
or a sequential discourse on detachment, or a non-sequential discourse on detachment.
[Commentary] "Successive" refers to the four propositions regarding the non-forgetting of mindfulness; "successive" also refers to the four propositions regarding the illumination of mindfulness.
Since forgetting and illuminating are fundamentally sought for the purpose of detachment from the three poisons, there are likewise four propositions regarding successive detachment.

If one grasps the meaning of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) of the Distinct Teaching (*bimiao jiao*), these propositions can be understood. Why is this? For instance, when illuminating emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one must necessarily forget emptiness in order to dispel it.

Because of attachment, one forgets illumination; those who achieve [enlightenment] must necessarily depart from both views and afflictions. Therefore, this contemplation of emptiness involves forgetting existence while maintaining illumination and departing [from delusion].
Subsequently, in the contemplations of the provisional and the middle, one must likewise discuss these three aspects: forgetting, illuminating, and departing.
If these are not practiced in sequence—forgetting, illuminating, and departing—this constitutes the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*), as in the four propositions mentioned above.
II. Summary of the Meaning and the Capacity of the Audience:

This is evident from the scriptural text. Because the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Immeasurable Meaning, possesses such great majestic spiritual power and brings benefit to so many, sentient beings should always keep him in mind.
Second, regarding the explanation based on the contemplation of the downward [view], there are two parts: first, the reference to the above for the first seven instances;
second, the explanation based on the contemplative understanding, where the seven instances may be understood by analogy with what precedes them. [Commentary]:

From the stage of retribution upward, including the Bodhisattvas of Shared [Teaching], none are able to break through the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) accumulation of suffering, as is the case for those of the Separate [Teaching].
Although [the offenses] were committed later, because they follow from the initial mind, they are pointed out as being the same as before.
○ Second, "Now, however," etc.: the latter three sections shall explain the two aspects—initial and subsequent—of the three poisons and the [five] rebellious acts in detail.
First, the dual designation regarding the realm beyond (dharmadhātu).

Now, we shall merely treat the two aspects of the direct and reverse orders according to the realm beyond (*dharmadhātu*). We do not take up the characteristics of the three poisons of the segmented [birth]. II.
Now, taking up the second section, the detailed explanation according to the characteristics of the Dharma, it is divided into two parts: first, showing the direct and reverse orders respectively;
second, the direct order explained in terms of afflictions. A. First, clarifying the poison and harm. 1. The three poisons of the Two Vehicles. a. First, clarifying the poison.
Regarding the first of the two aspects, the three poisons are explained together.
Now, taking the mind of wholesome desire as "greed," a great sutra states: "All wholesome dharmas have the desire for them as their root.
Desiring the bliss of nirvana is called greed; loathing birth-and-death is called hatred; and failing to realize this principle is called delusion.
Second, by opening up the three [poisons] and further opening them down, they become eighty thousand.
By opening up the three poisons, there are exactly eighty-four thousand [afflictions], fully and perfectly complete.
[Commentary: Since there are the three poisons, one must discuss their equal distribution; as each of the four parts possesses twenty-one thousand, for this reason—
Since it is thus within the eighty-four thousand realms, it is likewise so outside them. Why? Because the Mahāyāna teaches that all phenomena are not extinguished;
thus, when one speaks of severing delusions, it is merely the transformation of the out-flowing (sāsrava) into the non-out-flowing (anāsrava), entering the provisional and the middle.
These eighty-four thousand [realms] transform according to contemplation, and upon reaching fruition, they are termed the eighty-four thousand waves.
This is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Second, regarding the name "Pure," he cites a scripture as proof.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "If the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, flowers will adhere to the body; likewise, the two vehicles have not yet severed these three poisons."
This refers to the transformation of the characteristics of the three poisons.

[Commentary] In the "Chapter on Observing Sentient Beings," when the heavenly maidens scattered celestial flowers upon the various Bodhisattvas and Great Disciples, the flowers that reached the Bodhisattvas all fell away immediately;
however, when they reached the Great Disciples, they adhered and did not fall. All the disciples... [text continues].
The son [Śāriputra] used his supernatural power to remove the flowers, but was unable to make them go away. At that time, the goddess asked Śāriputra, "For what reason do you remove these flowers?
He replied, "These flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma; therefore, I remove them. The goddess said, "Do not say that these flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma.
Why is this? These flowers have no discrimination; it is you, O Venerable One, who give rise to discrimination."

"It was merely a thought," and so on, up to: "It is because their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been exhausted that the flowers cling to their bodies; for those whose habitual tendencies are exhausted, the flowers do not cling.

The commentary explains this by saying: "The fact that the flowers fall away upon reaching the stage of a Bodhisattva signifies that the Bodhisattva abides in the inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*), has already departed from the delusions of separation (*bhinna-kleśa*), and thus is not affected by the exquisite five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) of the *sambhoga-kāya* land."
Because they are able to move, the flowers do not adhere to their bodies and all fall away on their own; however, when it comes to the Great Disciples, the flowers adhere and do not fall.
This is because those of the Two Vehicles have only severed the five desires within the realm, and thus cannot be moved by the five worldly desires;

yet, because their secondary afflictions have not been eliminated, they are defiled by the superior and wondrous forms and sounds beyond the realm. Therefore, they are rebuked with the word "bondage" (*saṃyojana*).

If habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, the flowers will adhere to the body. Regarding this, the subsequent analysis asks: "If habitual tendencies are not yet exhausted, the flowers adhere to the body;

what does this have to do with the separate delusions (*pṛthag-moha*)? The answer is that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Śrāvaka sūtras, these are called 'habitual tendencies' (*vāsanā*);
in the Mahāyāna, they are called 'active afflictions' (*paryavasthāna*), which are precisely the separate delusions."
Second, regarding the three poisons of the lower bodhisattvas that have not yet been severed:

because bodhisattvas who have not yet severed their specific delusions likewise possess these three poisons, it is said that a bodhisattva’s greedy pursuit of the Buddha-dharma—never abandoning it for even a moment throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and never being satiated with extensive learning—is the characteristic of greed (rāga). This is the fault.
Because they despise the Two Vehicles and take no pleasure in hearing their names, it is said:

"It would be better to give rise to the mind of a wicked, leper-like jackal than to give rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles," as illustrated by the analogy of a great tree breaking its branches. Is this not the mark of anger?

The heavy accumulations of ignorance are many, yet they are all that can be severed by the wisdom of Buddha-enlightenment. That which has not yet fully realized the Buddha-nature is entirely the mark of delusion.
[Commentary] Those who equally possess these three poisons are called "the same" in relation to the two previous vehicles, yet the meaning differs. Previously, they were attached to emptiness;

now, they are attached to the conventional world. Previously, they were angry at saṃsāra; now, they are angry at nirvāṇa. Previously, they did not realize the Truth, which is the Middle Way, and thus it was ignorance;
now, although they see the Middle Way, they have not attained clear realization, and thus it is ignorance—just as when a large tree has its branches broken off.
Regarding the analogy, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 30, states:

"For example, in a vast marsh there was a tree named Śamālī, whose branches and twigs were broad and massive, and where many large birds gathered to roost. A single pigeon arrived last and perched upon one branch;
the branch immediately broke under its weight. The spirit of the marsh asked for the reason, and the tree spirit replied: 'This bird comes from the tree of my enemy.'"
"Come eat the seeds of that nyagrodha tree, or perch upon me; if you should void excrement and the seeds fall to the ground, that evil tree will grow again and its harm will surely be great.
Therefore, harboring such anxiety, it is better to break off a single branch so that what is preserved is greater.
This is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s fear that the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) will destroy the mind of the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna).

II. The second section, on the desire to eliminate [afflictions], clarifies the responsive engagement with sentient beings; it has two parts. First, clarifying the responsive engagement with sentient beings through right mindfulness:

Because one desires to eliminate these three afflictions, by constantly mindfuly recollecting Avalokiteśvara, he responds according to the capacities of sentient beings, whereby one immediately attains eternal liberation.
II. Permanently Free from the Lower [Realms]: This clarifies the entirety of the higher lands.

There are two types of "permanently free": if this Bodhisattva, within their birth-body (*janma-kāya*), has not yet entirely eliminated the specific afflictions (*pṛthag-āsrava*), then in terms of the transformation body (*pariṇāmi-kāya*), they are not yet permanently free;
if, within the birth-body, they have already begun to subdue the specific afflictions, then in terms of the transformation body—
"Eliminating the remnants means being eternally free from them.

[Commentary] Bodhisattvas in their birth-body (*janmakāya*) who have not yet attained entry into the stages (*bhūmi*) of the Separate or Perfect Teachings and thus dwell in the Land of Expedient Means (*upāyabhūmi*) have not at all been freed from the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*) regarding the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmikakāya*). However, those in their birth-body who have entered the stages and dwell therein...
Because it is born from the true retribution, residual distinct delusions are eliminated within the transformation;

thus, the distinction between the transformation land and the land of true retribution through skillful means arises solely from the difference in whether the birth-body has partially penetrated or not yet penetrated the delusion of ignorance.

Second, following the "Explanation of the Method of Inverse Correlation" (*nidāna-vyākhyāna-dharmamukha*) below the "Secondary Clarification": the reason for establishing the titles of the contemplative methods using the names of the afflictions (*kleśa*) rather than following the conventional path is termed "inverse teaching.
However, if one does not understand the principle of the inherent evil of nature (*prakṛti-pāpaka*), how could the three poisons (*triviṣa*) be taken as the three contemplations?

Within this section, there are two parts; first, it clarifies the contemplation of the poisons so that [the practice] may be accomplished. Within this, there are two further parts; first, it clarifies the poisons of ordinary beings and followers of the Two Vehicles.
Next, to clarify the contemplation of the three poisons through the method of inverse explanation: all sentient beings are said to have "few desires. Why is this?

It is because they cease the hatred that leads to the suffering of the three miserable realms and instead crave the pleasures of humans and devas; as for those of the Two Vehicles, they merely hate the cycle of birth and death.
All who desire to attain the bliss of *nirvāṇa* are said to have "little.
[Commentary] The Dharma is brief; for deluded persons, it is brief. For Bodhisattvas, delusion follows greed and hatred and is likewise called "little.
It is not that Bodhisattvas are biased toward the three poisons, but rather that these are not numerous [in their case].
II. Regarding the Bodhisattva below, this shows that the person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanren) has much poison. Part One: Discussing "Greatness" in terms of the name of poison.
The Bodhisattva is not like this; they joyfully seek the Buddha-dharma, seeking not merely one Buddha-dharma, but universally seeking all unspeakable Buddha-dharmas.
Like the ocean swallowing all streams yet never being filled, they do not merely refrain from undergoing birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, because one does not even accept *nirvāṇa*, as stated in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*: "The five non-acceptances are precisely great hatred.
The power of ignorance is so great that even the Buddha-wisdom can only sever it; yet the bodhisattva still remains amidst the delusions of this powerful ignorance.
Moreover, delusion is like space and cannot be exhausted, and even death is like space and cannot be exhausted.

[Commentary] The phrasing is roughly the same as before, but the meaning is fundamentally different. Previously, within the context of the two truths (*dvayasatya*), one discussed taking and rejecting based on partial arguments regarding dharmas that can be abandoned.
Now, speaking from the perspective of the three truths (*trisatya*), greed, hatred, and delusion are explained according to the ultimate principle:

since the poison of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) is omnipresent, they are all termed "great. Regarding "non-acceptance" (*anupādāna*): it means neither accepting acceptance, nor accepting non-acceptance.
"Not receiving," "both receiving and not receiving," "neither receiving nor not receiving," and "not even the non-receiving of non-receiving"—all these are called "non-receiving.
This refers to the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-darśana*), which sweeps away grasping and attachment.

The first four [positions] are the departure from the four extremes (*catuṣkoṭi*); the last one means that even the contemplation itself vanishes. Thus it is said in the second chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti why he did not accept [the gift], and Subhūti replied: "Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is empty, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not accept.
Below this, it clarifies that the poison of delusion (*moha*) is identical to its nature; the discussion of its nature differs from what preceded, as it pertains solely to cultivation.
Furthermore, below the section on delusion, it clarifies that if delusion and the like were not identical to their nature, how could they all be like space and thus inexhaustible?
II. Regarding the section "In this way," the wondrousness is elucidated by means of the Dharma-gates. First, the three gates are presented:
these three poisons are themselves three Dharma-gates—first, grasping; second, relinquishing; and third, neither grasping nor relinquishing.
[Commentary]: The dharma-virtues of the principle-nature transcend all limits; they may be termed "poisonous harm" or "efficacious function.
Herein it is clarified that the three poisons are three dharma-gates, which all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cultivate and realize.

II. Regarding "The Two Great Compassions" and below, this explains the three aspects: the contemplation of the objects of the three poisons of view and thought as being perfectly integrated, wherein the three dharma-gates encompass all virtues.
Part III: First, the Dharma-gate of Great Greed.
Great kindness and great compassion, the four means of integration, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, samādhi, liberation, unsurpassed bodhi, purifying buddha-fields,
and transforming and delivering sentient beings— these are called the "gate of grasping," which is precisely great greed.

[Commentary] Regarding "Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion": the Buddhas universally permeate the three karmas with unconditioned (anālambana) loving-kindness and compassion throughout the worlds of the ten directions, manifesting form-bodies to perform Buddha-works.
Although the names "loving-kindness" and "compassion" are the same as those found among the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), their essence is eternally distinct from them.
The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are: first, giving (*dāna*); second, kind speech (*priyavāditā*); third, beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*); [and fourth, common purpose].
The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) encompass the inclinations of sentient beings; that which is beloved by them consists precisely of these four dharmas.

By means of these four, one receives and guides them, delivering and liberating them through the Right Path. As for the ten powers (*daśabala*): first is the power of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*);

second is the power of karma (*karma-bala*); third is the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*); fourth is the power of the faculties (*indriya-bala*); fifth is the power of inclinations (*adhimukti-bala*); sixth is the power of dispositions (*dhātu-bala*); seventh is the power of the path leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-bala*).

The powers are: (1) the power of knowing what is possible and impossible, (2) the power of knowing the ripening of karma, (3) the power of knowing various inclinations, (4) the power of knowing various dispositions, (5) the power of knowing the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and equanimities, (6) the power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations, (7) the power of recollecting past lives, (8) the power of the divine eye, and (9) the power of the exhaustion of outflows.

The fearlessnesses are the four types of intrepidity: (1) fearlessness regarding possessing all-knowledge, (2) fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows, (3) fearlessness regarding teaching the obstacles to the path, and (4) fearlessness regarding teaching the path that leads to the end of suffering. Among these eight assemblies, he extensively proclaims his own and others' [attainments].
Since wisdom and abandonment are definitive and free from error, there is not even the slightest sign of fear; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Fearlessness.
The explanations for all one hundred and eight samādhis are as set forth in the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm).
II. The Section on Great Anger.
All dharmas are empty and non-existent; they neither abide nor are they attached to. Prajñā is like a great conflagration, which cannot be grasped from any of its four sides.
Great Nirvāṇa is empty, as is the city of Kapilavastu; it is where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases.
Extinction is not attained through the four propositions; that there is neither attainment nor realization is the gate of relinquishment, which is called "great anger.
[Commentary] Prajñā refers to the three types of prajñā. That which cannot be grasped from the four extremes is the *pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā* (contemplative wisdom), which is quiescence.

The wisdom of illumination (*prajñā-prakāśa*) cannot be grasped through existence; the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*), which is both illumination and quiescence, cannot be grasped through emptiness;
the wisdom of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa-prajñā*), which is neither quiescent nor illuminating, cannot be grasped by taking both together;
and that which is both quiescent and illuminating cannot be grasped by negating both. This is as recorded in the *Xuanji* regarding the city of Kapilavastu.

Regarding the three gates of great delusion (*mahāmoha-dharmamukha*), although both the gate of grasping and the gate of relinquishing possess the Middle Way, the gate of grasping ultimately takes the establishment of dharmas as its tenet, while the gate of relinquishing ultimately takes the eradication of marks as its primary focus.

Now, do these two gates of relinquishing not likewise possess the two extremes? Yet they ultimately take non-duality as their essence; thus, while not three, they appear as three, and the two gates remain distinct and clear.
Regarding the three yet not-three gates, their wondrousness is absolute. First, by means of non-conditioning, it is directly revealed:
the Middle Way is neither grasping nor rejecting, neither hating nor loving, neither annihilating nor eternalizing, neither departing nor arriving, and neither arising nor ceasing.
Second, the difficulty of conceiving the reflected image in a mirror:
Just as a reflection in a mirror cannot be seen and yet is seen, and though seen it cannot be seen— it is neither visible nor invisible—
because it excludes the two extremes, it is ineffable.
Third, citing the silence of Vimalakīrti:
Vimalakīrti’s silence is called the Middle Way; this is precisely "great delusion.
Third, citing human testimony as a conclusion.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī said: "I am the śrī of desire, the śrī of hatred, and the śrī of wrong views.
This is the clear evidence.
[Commentary] The *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra* states: The sons of the gods addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, Mañjuśrī..."
Named Unobstructed Śrī, Supreme Śrī, and Peerless Śrī, Mañjuśrī spoke to the devaputras, saying:
"Stop, stop, O devaputras! Do not grasp at signs or engage in conceptual discrimination. I do not perceive any phenomena as superior, middling, or inferior, such as you have described.
As for the meaning of 'Śrī' according to my teaching, O devaputras, I am the Śrī of desire, the Śrī of hatred, and the Śrī of delusion."
"Śiri is ignorance; Śiri is therefore my name Mañjuśrī. He continued, "I am an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);
I arise from desire, I arise from hatred, and I arise from ignorance. I am a follower of external paths (*tīrthika*) and a practitioner of heterodox ways.
The devaputras asked, "For what reason do you say of yourself that you are an ordinary person and so forth? [The text continues with the explanation.]
Mañjuśrī said: "This nature of greed, hatred, and delusion cannot be found by seeking it throughout the ten directions.
Because I abide in this nature through the dharma of non-abiding, I say of myself: 'I am an ordinary person. Mañjuśrī, why do you call me a follower of external paths?
Mañjuśrī replied: "I have never entered the various paths of externalists; because the nature of those paths cannot be apprehended, I—[regarding myself]..."
"All paths are external. The various devaputras asked, "How is it that you are a practitioner of the heterodox?
Mañjuśrī replied, "I have already known that all dharmas are heterodox, empty, false, and unreal; therefore, I am a practitioner of the heterodox.
When he said these words, ten thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

II. Regarding the desire to fulfill the lower [levels], one constantly contemplates the responsive resonance (*pratibhāsa*). First, it clarifies that when the capacity (*karana*) is perfected, the virtue is fulfilled:
if one desires to fulfill these three dharma-gates, by constantly contemplating Avalokiteśvara, one shall immediately obtain the fulfillment of one's vows.
Second, the section below on "All" clarifies that which all sages rely upon.
There is no practice for self-cultivation or transforming others among all sages that does not enter through these three gates;
apart from these, there is no other path.
Third, there is no citation from the *Apracāra-sūtra* as proof.
Thus, the *Apracāra-sūtra* states: "Lust is itself the Way; hatred and delusion are likewise.
Within these three dharmas, all Buddha-dharmas are fully contained."
Fourth, all that follows concludes with the Buddha-dharma.
All Buddha-dharmas do not transcend the vast function of the myriad practices, the *pāramitās*, the *samādhis* of non-attainment,
and the Middle Way of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
II. Regarding these three [teachings], the following section discusses them in both forward and reverse order. First, the dual demonstration for the sake of sentient beings:

These three dharma-gates cannot be definitively proclaimed; out of compassion for sentient beings, they are sometimes taught in forward order and sometimes in reverse order, with mutual inclusion and exclusion.
This is precisely the intent of the four *siddhāntas*, providing benefit by responding to conditions.

[Commentary] To constantly mindfully seek liberation from the three afflictions is called "conformable teaching" (anuloma). To constantly mindfully seek fulfillment through the three dharma-gates is called "inverse teaching" (pratiloma).
Fulfillment and liberation occur simultaneously; it is merely according to the *siddhānta* that they are spoken of in terms of being taken or rejected.
II. Regarding the *Avataṃsaka*, the following scriptural passages provide detailed evidence in three parts. First, the proof concerning the transgression and compliance of desire:

As clarified in the forty-second fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, in the city of Ratnavyūha within the perilous land, the woman Vasumitrā expounds the Dharma-gate of the Limit of Freedom from Desire (*vairāgyakoṭi*).
It states that all sentient beings perceive her according to their respective types, and she appears as a woman to each of them.
Those who see me shall attain the Samādhi of Joy; those who converse with me shall attain the Samādhi of Unobstructed Wondrous Sound;
those who grasp my hand shall attain the Samādhi of Traveling to All Buddha-fields; those who stay overnight with me shall attain the Samādhi of the Light of Liberation;
those who gaze upon me with their eyes shall attain the Dharma-gate of Quiescence; and those who witness my frequent sighs shall attain the Destruction and Dispersion of External [Defilements].
In this Dharma-gate of the Path, "Ā-li-yi-wo" (Ariya) signifies the attainment of the Samādhi that gathers all sentient beings;
"A-zhong-bi-wo" (Ajñāpaka) signifies dwelling in the secret treasury of all merits. Abiding in this Dharma-gate of detachment from desire, one extensively brings benefit to others.
Is this not the Dharma-gate of following and reversing desire, which guides and benefits all classes of beings?
[Commentary: To speak of "leaving the limit of desire" (*kāma-anta-vivikta*) is to follow the favorable; to see a woman [in that context] is to follow the contrary.
Since desire is an affliction (*kleśa*), it is said that "leaving desire" is a Dharma-gate. Therefore, it is said that "abiding is itself leaving" and "leaving is itself abiding.

Only by leaving can one abide; only by abiding can one leave. Leaving deeply is profound abiding; leaving to the ultimate is ultimate abiding. Now, Avalokiteśvara is precisely one who abides at the ultimate limit, having left behind lustful desire.
Therefore, all those who seek liberation from craving and those who seek to dwell [in it] must constantly maintain mindfulness.
Second, furthermore, the following four sections below demonstrate the transgressions and compliance regarding anger.
Furthermore, in the city of Ekādaśa-pūrṇadhvaja, King Pūrṇabhadra was administering the royal law in the main hall when one who had violated the law...
[He] executed [criminals] by beheading, burning, boiling, cleaving, splitting, and slaughtering; he rebuked them with glaring eyes and punished them with cruel torments. Sudhana became suspicious.
After the King had finished adjudicating the case, he took Sudhana by the hand and entered his palace, where he beheld an inconceivable realm beyond all metaphors.
He said to Sudhana: "I know the dharma-gate of illusory transformation (*māyā-nirmāṇa*), by which I manifest as sentient beings."
Yet, one treats them with harsh discipline to harmonize all those who see or hear it, causing them to give rise to the bodhicitta;
is this not the dharma-gate of anger?

[Commentary: "To harmonize all" refers to those who are compliant; "to treat with harsh punishment" refers to those who are rebellious. Because resentment, harm, and afflictions exist, [this practice is necessary].
The Dharma-gate for subduing anger and hatred must therefore involve practicing the non-dual discipline of both contrariness and conformity without partiality;

this principle is the same as that previously applied to greed. However, because greed is a pleasant phenomenon, one engages with others through actual deeds to cause them to leave behind hatred and harm.

Because hatred is a painful phenomenon, one subdues others through illusory means to cause them to leave it behind. If the karmic conditions are such that it is appropriate to [use other means], one should do so.
As for those who gain benefit through actual killing, this is like the case of Xianyu, who killed a Brahmin as a gateway to the Dharma of *dveṣa* (hatred).

This is an example of the mutual manifestation of the provisional and the real; it may likewise be established as an illusion in the cases of greed and delusion. It is sufficient merely to grasp the principle that the adverse and the favorable are mutually identical, regardless of whether the act is provisional or real.
Third, the lower section on the expedient means for verifying the conventional and ultimate nature of ignorance:
The expedient means of commanding a brahmin to perform the "five-fold heat-torment" (*pañcatapa*) is precisely a dharma-gate of ignorance, as previously explained.

[Commentary] As with the previous "fire disaster," the full scriptural passages are cited; the sequence of fulfillment and transcendence follows the pattern of the preceding two poisons, as their meaning is no different.
○ Second, from "next" below, the two contemplations of compassion are explained by analogy with what precedes.

Next, one should clarify the distinct and perfect contemplations (*bieyuan lianguan*). The principles for contemplating the three poisons and responding to the capacities of sentient beings through compassion can be understood by analogy;
they are not recorded here in full.

[Commentary] The Great Being originally cultivated the contemplation of fulfilling the three poisons and then departing from them; furthermore, he beheld sentient beings being afflicted by the transgressions of the three poisons.

Regarding those who are afflicted and harmed, one also perceives that they wish to fulfill the dharmas of the three poisons; therefore, one gives rise to compassion and vows to cause sentient beings to leave behind the faults of the three poisons and fulfill their virtues.

Now, having become a candidate for Buddhahood (anāgāmin) adjacent to the ultimate state because of the three poisons, one is able to act spontaneously throughout the entire dharma-realm, universally causing all sentient beings to fulfill, depart from, and achieve [the realization of] these [virtues]. Thus, both gradual and sudden contemplations are [applied].

Regarding the contemplation of the three poisons: if sudden, one contemplates them as being fully encompassed by non-duality; if gradual, the initial mind contemplates only their separation, and only later does it contemplate their full separation, wherein the aspect of separation is identical with illumination.

The text is divided into two parts: first, the fulfillment of the prayer; second, the concluding praise of the prayer. The latter is further divided into two: first, the request for a son; second, the request for a daughter.
Regarding the second section, the text below provides a detailed analysis, beginning with the question concerning the solitary daughter’s request for a son.
The text states: "If a woman seeks a son, should she be childless, the lineage will be severed; if she has a son, both parents will rejoice.
Why, then, does it single out only the woman seeking a son?"
Regarding the second part, the explanation of the suffering of women who have no sons, there are two sections. First, the erroneous interpretations of others:

some explain that this refers to women who loathe their female bodies and do not seek sons; others explain that because women generally possess much affection and place particular importance on the joy of having children, the text specifically singles out "women."
II. Now, the second section: explaining the subsequent correct interpretation.
This explains that for a woman, being childless is a source of suffering: she is abandoned by her husband, held in contempt by her wife, and ridiculed by others.
Furthermore, among the seven faults of a wife, six may yet be endured, but being childless is the most severe; it includes having a foul disposition and being jealous.

Being unable to serve one's parents-in-law, being greedy for food, having no son, or being clumsy and having no son—because these are hardships, they are cited here as the reasons women seek a male child.

II. Explaining the Seeking of a Daughter, Part Two: First, the Citation of the Sūtra.
If one wishes to seek a daughter, she shall be born upright and endowed with auspicious marks; having planted roots of virtue in past lives, she will be loved and respected by all people.
II. Regarding the second section, "Seeking a Wife," the commentary below is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies the intention behind the inclusion and omission of certain elements.
In the text concerning the seeking of a wife, only the vows and virtuous deeds are explained, while the practice of cultivation is not.

II. Regarding the section on the two women, this clarifies the meaning of appearance (*lakṣaṇa*).

Physical beauty is the first of the seven virtues; however, if one possesses beauty without [auspicious] marks (*nimitta*), one may become orphaned early or widowed young, as the fortune indicated by such marks is not favorable.
Here, it is clarified that appearance and marks support one another to further manifest virtue; thus, physical beauty brings about [favorable results].
The marks of being cherished and loved bring forth fortune and respect; therefore, the text says that the multitude loves and respects [the Buddha].
If one were to love with arrogance, how could it be called virtue? It is precisely because one loves and respects him that these marks appear.

If the parents’ wisdom and physical perfection were due to the child’s past planting of roots [of merit],

[Commentary] These two phrases, "having planted the roots of virtue in the past" and "loved and respected by all," according to their meaning, still refer to the woman.
Regarding the passage concerning the "subduing of doubts" by both male and female [bodhisattvas], other masters erroneously claim it provides a dual explanation.

My intention is that people might suspect that the wisdom of the male and the physical perfection of the female are both obtained through the cultivation of the causes of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), rather than being bestowed by a Sage or acquired without cultivation;

○ Second, the private objection below clarifies the current correct principle. Part two: Refuting the objection. First, the objection based on establishing one's own position.
The private objection states: "If these words mean that merit and wisdom are the karma of the child, then Avalokiteśvara can only bring about his taking of birth."
If a child lacks the conditions for birth, how can Avalokiteśvara cause them to be born? If they lack merit and wisdom, how can Avalokiteśvara even enable them to possess them?

If he cannot cause what is absent to exist, how can he cause what exists to cease? If one argues that merit must be cultivated to produce merit, how can one claim that what is non-existent can be produced?

Furthermore, regarding the fear of falling into the theory of uncaused existence (*ahetuvāda*) through the practice of ritual prostration—if one fears falling into the theory of uncaused existence when it comes to birth, why does one not likewise fear falling into the theory of uncaused existence when it comes to [the cessation of] birth? If this were so, the Sage would be entirely incapable of bestowing anything.
That merit and wisdom can only act as matchmakers— this is incomprehensible.
[Commentary] Since the taking of birth by merit and wisdom both depends on conditions, and since Avalokiteśvara is already able to provide the conditions for their birth,
why could he not also provide the conditions for merit and wisdom?
II. Second, the refutation by citing scriptural passages to challenge the difficulty of contemplation.

This challenges the claim that Avalokiteśvara cannot bestow merit and wisdom upon children: if one person’s mere invocation of his name can cause many people to escape the peril of rākṣasas, why does he not grant this here when there is no such cause?
And why do those who lack the requisite capacity suddenly escape [the danger]?
[Commentary]: If a child does not cultivate the causes, even a Sage cannot bestow upon them merit and wisdom; if the multitude does not praise one’s name, how can one attain liberation?
This is explained through the present text to refute the attachment to causelessness. It is not by means of a conceptual interpretation that those of like mind seek blessings.
II. Now, to clarify the following: the formal establishment of the two [points]. First, the explanation:
We now clarify that the power of the Sage is exceedingly great; there is nothing he does not grant, being able to cause those who possessed merit and wisdom in previous lives to take rebirth.
Even if one did not plant roots of goodness in previous lives, he can still cause them to cultivate practice within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
This meaning of "merit" (*puṇya*) is derived from the *Antarābhava-sūtra*. [Commentary:

Avalokiteśvara’s activity pervades the Dharma-realm of the three thousandfold world system. For those among sentient beings who have attained great mastery over the conditions for non-arising, he causes them to plant the conditions for arising;
even for those who lack the merit and wisdom to do so, he is able to cause them to plant [the seeds]. All such [activities] occur within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Because it is produced within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the *Antarābhava Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata Sublime Enlightenment (*Sujñāna*), by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*), leads the immeasurable fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings into the intermediate state, where he transforms [the place] into lecture halls of the seven treasures, seats of the seven treasures, and so forth.

He causes all those sentient beings in the intermediate state—whether their lives were to end after seven days or down to a single day—to remain for the full duration of their lifespans, and the Tathāgata bestows [upon them]..."
The manifested Buddha preaches the Dharma to transform and instruct seven trillion eight hundred billion nayutas of beings in the intermediate state,
causing them to give rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment. As the sutra explains at great length,
if he can cause those beings in the intermediate state to generate the bodhicitta, how could he not enable them to plant the roots of merit and wisdom?

"If one pays homage, the merit is never in vain"—this concludes the discussion on the conditions for bodily action (*kāyakarman*) and also serves to resolve doubts.

Regarding the meaning of "not in vain": this phrase can resolve doubts. If one says that while fulfilling a vow through prostration depends on the vow itself, there are cases where one performs prostrations yet does not receive the fulfillment of the vow—how then can it be said that [the act] is not in vain?
"In vain" (*táng*) means empty or futile; "vain" (*juān*) means discarded or abandoned.
This occurs when the mind lacks resolve, and thus the vow remains unfulfilled. However, the merit of the prostration is secretly sustained and not lost; this is what constitutes being "not in vain."
This explains away doubts.
