If one proceeds from the stage of Subtle Enlightenment, it constitutes the marks of the complete reward-body, with its physical characteristics, radiance, and immeasurable light, identical to those of the [Buddhas of the ten directions]. ○ First, the Land of Real Reward.
For the sentient beings of the Land of True Reward on the First Ground, he preaches the Dharma of the Single Truth of Ultimate Reality to transform them;
such a response is not something that other realms can endure.

[Commentary] Regarding the perfection of the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), it is as explained in the "Chapter on the Ocean of Tathāgata Marks" and the "Chapter on the Radiance of the Minor Marks" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,

which state that there are marks numbering as many as the atoms within ten lotus-treasury worlds (*padma-garbha-loka-dhātu*), each adorned with exquisite characteristics. As for the teaching of the Single Truth (*eka-satyatva*),

if one approaches it from the perspective of the Path of Teaching (*śikṣā-mārga*), even within the true retribution (*satya-vipāka*) there are still those who rely on the faculties and conditions of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*).
The exposition of the immeasurable Four Noble Truths is now discussed according to the ultimate reality.
II. Demonstrating the Appropriate Capacity:
Why is this so? Because these various stages have already been differentiated as levels of attainment; it is not possible to respond with a body belonging to another realm.
Furthermore, one must not think that other Buddha-bodies should respond in this same manner; for such a response is appropriate only for that particular land and cannot be sustained by other lands.
[Commentary] Since the forty-one stages all share the same essence and function as the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), they cannot be categorized according to the nine realms.
His body corresponds to the inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇakāya*).

○ Second, "Furthermore, below there are two remaining [sections]": first, the discussion on existence and non-existence; second, the existence and non-existence according to the Great and Small Vehicles.

Furthermore, regarding the Manifestation Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*) as explained in the land of transformation (*pariṇāmikabhūmi*), the Sūtras of the Small Vehicle state that there is no birth outside the three realms.

Only by mounting the five kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*) does one take birth in the Land of Expedient Means; this is precisely the Land of Transformation-Birth where one undergoes birth beyond the three realms.

[Commentary] Both the Land of Expedient Means and the Land of True Reward involve transformation-birth (*parināmikī-jarāmaraṇa*), yet this one alone is singled out for such a name because it is the superior land.

In this context, the designation "partial" (*fenpo*) depends entirely on what is designated according to its dominant factor. The Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) does not speak of a permanently abiding Buddha-nature;

thus, when the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) are exhausted, the retributive fruit (*vipākaphala*) perishes forever. Because the Mahāyāna speaks of permanence, it establishes three lands beyond the triple world (*tridhātu*).

When ignorance (*avidyā*) is completely destroyed, one dwells in the Land of Peaceful Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*); when it is partially destroyed, one dwells in the Land of True Retribution (*bhūtaniṣyanda*); and when it is fully present, one dwells in the Land of Residual Existence (*sopadhiśeṣa*). These constitute the five kinds [of lands].

The mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) is that which is entirely present; while the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* clarifies only three types of mind-made bodies, our school expands them into five based on their meaning.
As for the three types: first, the body formed by the attainment of the bliss of samādhi, which corresponds to the mind-set of the Two Vehicles entering emptiness;
second, the body formed by the awakening to the self-nature of dharmas, which corresponds to the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*).

The Bodhisattva’s emergence from the provisional [state] involves three types of co-arising non-conceptual mental attention (*amanasikāra*); this simulates the middle-grade mental attention cultivated by Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*).
If expanded into five, one opens two teachings for the two vehicles within the samādhi, and for the awakening to dharmas, one opens the ten practices (*daśa-pratipatti*) of the Separate Teaching;
alternatively, seven types may be made, with each of the two vehicles of the two teachings being opened.

Regarding why the separate teaching (*biejiao*) ten abidings (*shizhu*) are not mentioned for these two [stages], it is because their meaning is the same as that of the two vehicles entering emptiness.

If one discusses the nine types of people being born in the land of expedient means (*fangbian*), this further includes the separate teaching ten abidings and the perfect teaching (*yuanjiao*) ten faiths (*shixin*), which are subsumed within the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*yi-sheng-shen*).
Because they have not yet severed ignorance (*avidyā*) and have not yet produced the true retribution (*shibao*), they are collectively referred to as "mind-made."
This is because those who have not yet manifested the Truth all achieve [their realization] through intentional effort (*manasikāra*);
since their arising proceeds from the fruit, this is explained by summarizing the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Commentary) along with the *Fuxing* (Aids to Practice).
○ Second, the interpretation of the treatise: the definitive judgment according to the sutras and śāstras below.
The *Śāstra* states: "The Dharma-nature body (dharmatākāya) bodhisattvas are born outside the triple world; since they already have birth, how could they not have a response-body (nirmāṇakāya)?
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "I become a Buddha in other lands under different names"—this is precisely that meaning.
II. This section below clarifies the two aspects of the capacity and the response. First, it clarifies that there are only two types of responses shown.

These responses of the Buddha consist of two aspects: first, manifesting the perfect marks and oceans of characteristics of the superior response-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), as previously described regarding the response of true retribution;
second, manifesting the inferior response so that those who see it perceive it as inferior to the former, serving merely as the two Buddhas [of the two realms], and nothing more.
He manifests as various kinds of bodies. [Commentary:

First, regarding the manifestation of the Supreme Response Body (*sambhogakāya*): if one asks why this response body—which was previously described as the True Reward Body—is said here to be not capable of reaching other lands, yet is described as possessing the "ocean of perfect marks" as before, the answer is that while that [previous] response body corresponds to the true capacity of its specific audience, this [present] response body... [is for a different capacity].

When [the response] is joined with this [condition], it should resemble the case where the stimulus and the response have not yet met; at that time, one still applies mental attention (*manasikāra*), whereas the other acts according to its true nature (*tattva*).

Since the capacity to see is already distinct, how could the object seen be the same? It is simply because this stimulus has already suppressed or partially eliminated ignorance (*avidyā*) that the retributive characteristics (*vipākalinga*) are employed to draw one into the truth.
To say "as before" is merely a partial resemblance to the true retribution (*sambhoga-nirmāṇa*); it does not mean they are entirely identical.

Question: Regarding the two manifestations of the Inferior Response Body (*hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya*) shown by a single Buddha in this land, how do their superior and inferior appearances compare with the *vairocana* (Universal Radiance) and *mānuṣī* (human-like) forms of the Shared Dwelling Land? Answer:

The two types of response through skillful means (*upāya*) merely explain the sequential and non-sequential [teachings]. As for the second category, the Mahāyāna, there are five kinds of *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made bodies).

Although those who receive the teachings differ in their capacities—whether sharp or dull—since they have all received the Mahāyāna, they all know that the Buddha’s wisdom is the nature of the Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi).
Those who can cultivate Madhyamaka and subdue ignorance are superior in their perception of the marks [of the Buddha];

if one remains within the two [lower] contemplations and has not yet subdued ignorance, their perception of the marks is inferior. Although these perceptions may be superior or inferior, they refer to the same single Honored One; therefore, it is not so.
Regarding the "combined body" (*he-shen*): when the Shared Teaching is expounded in the same land, those of dull faculties perceive only emptiness and thus manifest the sixteen-foot form;

those of sharp faculties perceive non-emptiness and thus manifest the *zuntè* (exalted) form. Because these two types of capacities—large and small—have differing views and understandings regarding a single Buddha-body, they are called the "sixteen-foot" and "exalted" combined body.
This [Pure Land] is exclusively perceived as the Great [Vehicle], and therefore it is not called "combined."
II. Why [the teaching] below clarifies that it is intended solely for two types of faculties. Part 1: General Demonstration.

Why is this so? Because there are distinctions between the sharp and dull faculties of the five kinds of *manomayakāya* (mind-made bodies), and because these respond to such root-natures, only the two bodies are shown;
furthermore, since only the two types of Mahāyāna—those with sequential and non-sequential [attainment]—are taught, there is no need for other bodies or other dharmas to transform them.
...also. ○ Second, the detailed exposition regarding those of the Perfect [Teaching] and others:

If a person of the Perfect [Teaching] has not yet shattered their ignorance, or has only partially shattered it, they are at the stage of dedication (pariṇāmanā) among those of the Separate [Teaching], or have partially [shattered it].
Those who have destroyed ignorance are born in that land as individuals of sharp faculties;

however, those who have not yet cultivated or subdued their afflictions, those of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇayāna) who have severed delusions, and those of the Tripitaka Teaching (Śrāvakayāna) who have severed delusions—all such individuals are of dull faculties when born there.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement that "the person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanren) has not yet shattered ignorance," this refers to those from the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*) upward.
As for "partial shattering," the *Renwang Banruo Jing* states that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) consist of thirty grades;

since each stage itself contains three grades, we know that all forty-two positions of the Perfect Saint (*yuan-sheng*) likewise possess three grades. The three grades of the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) correspond to the tenth [stage].
One employs the contemplation of the three minds to counteract and break [the afflictions]: the first mind employs the contemplation to counteract and break the superior grade;

once that is broken, the middle mind employs the contemplation to counteract and break the middle grade; and once that is broken, the final mind employs the contemplation to counteract and break the inferior grade.

Only when this grade is broken is one said to have attained the First Abode (Prathamā-bhūmi) and been born into the Land of True Reward (Sambhoga-kṣetra). What is now being discussed is the partial breaking [of these grades].
"Furthermore, the arising of skillful means refers to the final mind within the tenth stage of faith (*śraddhā*).

For example, one who is like a person of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) abides in this final mind and passes through many kalpas before finally destroying the lower grade [of delusion] to realize entry into Sublime Enlightenment (*suyajñāna*).

The nine preceding stages and the initial mind of the tenth stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) are all termed 'not yet having destroyed' [the tenth]. Within the tenth stage of Dedication, the latter two minds are termed 'partially destroyed.'"

Both the Complete (Yuan) and the Separate (Bie) [teachings] cultivate the Middle Way to subdue and destroy ignorance; although they arise as skillful means, their faculties are already sharp, and thus they elicit a superior body of a Buddha and are taught the Perfect-Sudden Dharma.

From the seventh stage of the Separate teaching up to the tenth stage of the Practice (Xing), as well as the Bodhisattvas of the Shared (Tong) [teaching], focus exclusively on the conventional (the provisional);
the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the Treasured (Zang) and Shared [teachings] focus exclusively on emptiness. These beings are born within the stage of skillful means.

There are others who, although they already know [the truth], still constantly seek the Buddha’s wisdom; yet they remain obstructed by the two extremes and have not yet observed or subdued the delusions of ignorance.
Since their faculties are dull, they receive only inferior bodies and are taught the gradual dharma.

○ Third, the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages, also called the Land of Common Abode for the Pure and the Impure. This refers to the fact that both pure lands and impure lands each contain ordinary beings and sages who dwell together therein.
This explanation is divided into two parts: first, explaining the characteristics; second, [the specific analysis].

Regarding the first, there are two sections: first, a general clarification of the two lands and the two faculties; second, first, clarifying the two characteristics as they are experienced. Regarding the first of these, there are the two lands: the pure and the impure.
Regarding the Manifestation-Buddhas of the Land of Common Dwelling for All Saints and Worldlings, there are two types of lands: first, the pure; second, the defiled.

For example, the land of Pūrṇa and other lands in the western direction: the sentient beings therein possess the three poisons and the afflictions of views and thoughts, yet they lack the names of the three evil realms, and their karmic retribution is strictly pure;
this is called a pure land. In contrast, this Sahā world has the three evil realms and the four destinies, and is filled with thorns and brambles.

"Hills and mounds" refers to the defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-bhūmi*). Whether pure or defiled, all such lands are "lands where ordinary beings and sages dwell together" (*prthagjana-ārya-sahavāsa-bhūmi*).
[Commentary] Regarding the purity and defilement of lands, there are both horizontal and vertical dimensions.

If one defines purity and defilement by contrasting the *paricchinna-bhava* (limited, segmented existence) with the *pariṇāmi-bhava* (transformative existence), this is explained from a vertical perspective based on whether the pervasive delusions (*paryavasthāna-kleśa*) have been exhausted or not. As the *Śāstra* says: "To emerge..."
Beyond the three realms, there are pure lands where śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are born.

If one speaks of purity and impurity regarding the *pariccheda* (segmented) realm of birth-and-death, this refers to a horizontal comparison based on the relative lightness or heaviness of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
Now, by contrasting the Land of Ultimate Bliss and the Land of Good Purity with the Sahā world, this is a horizontal rather than a vertical comparison; therefore, these pure lands are visible.

The "poison" of conceptual thought refers to the absence of the name of the evil realms; since it is not poison but rather the cause of suffering, the two turbidities of views and afflictions are lightened.
As for the purity of the karmic retribution, the lifespan of the kalpa is lightened. What disparaging title could there be for sentient beings dwelling here?

Because they are gathered by the vows and practices of Amitābha, these [evils] are lightened; it is not that one must sever delusions to be born therein. Within this land, even those who commit the five heinous crimes through worldly benevolence and charity [are saved].
Because even the naming of the Buddha can give rise [to such states], the defiled characteristics of the Sahā world are evident to direct perception;
this is a discussion of the two lands, pure and impure, wherein both lands contain ordinary beings and sages. Ordinary beings are as previously described. Sages are of two kinds:
those who come as response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and those who attain through cultivation; this is the case for both lands.
Second, regarding the sharpness or dullness of the two faculties:
the sentient beings of the two lands each possess two types of faculties—those with sharp faculties yet heavy defilements, and those with dull faculties yet heavy defilements;
those with sharp faculties and light defilements, and those with dull faculties and light defilements.

[Commentary]: In lands of heavy defilement, there are naturally those with sharp and dull faculties regarding the root for awakening; in lands of light defilement, there are likewise those with sharp and dull faculties.
Because the land is contrasted with the faculty, four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) are formed.
Regarding the lightness and heaviness of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*):

those for whom the turbidities are heavy are like the sentient beings of the Sahā world, whose physical forms are ugly, deformed, stunted, and diminutive, whose lifespan ends at eighty years or even earlier through untimely death, whose afflictions (*kleśa*) are fiercely blazing, whose views and mental states are powerful, and whose seasons and times are coarse and perilous; this is what is meant.
The five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya) are heavy; the Pure Land is not so, which means the five turbidities are light.

[Commentary] From "the physical form" down to "most lowly and small" refers to the turbidity of sentient beings (sattva-kaṣāya); "the seasons and times being coarse and perilous" refers to the turbidity of the eon (kalpa-kaṣāya). The remaining three names are manifest.
Regarding "the Pure Land is not so," as the *Daben shu* (Commentary on the Mahāyāna Sūtra) asks: "Since it is said there are five turbidities, which ones [are absent]?"
These five purities correspond to the five impurities; the three poisons of the heterodox are the five impurities, while the orthodox are the five purities.
Since the pure lands of other directions lack the heterodox three poisons, the five hindrances there are light.
II. Why, below, does it clarify the two types of karma that can produce [rebirth]?
Why is it that those who do not cultivate much merit are born in a heavy and turbid land, while those who cultivate much merit are born in a light land?
[Commentary] What is called "merit" refers to the three kinds of merit. As stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*:
"First, filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders, possessing a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, and practicing the ten wholesome actions;
second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges, fully observing the various precepts, and not violating dignified conduct; third, generating the bodhicitta deeply..."

Faith in cause and effect, reading and reciting the Mahāyāna, and exhorting practitioners to advance—these three types of karma are the direct causes for the pure lands of the Buddhas of the three periods.
The commentary on that [text] states: "The first karma is shared with ordinary beings; the second is shared with those of the Two Vehicles;
the third is the uncommon karma of the Mahāyāna. That sutra says: "Those who wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss should cultivate these three."
Because of merit, it is said here that "cultivating much merit" and "not cultivating much merit" constitute the practices of the two lands;
this is discussed in terms of such merit.
○ Second, "If [the land is] defiled," etc., specifically indicates the two faculties of the defiled land. First, indicating the four propositions regarding the vehicle and the precepts. Second...
First, the characteristics of the categories are established:
those born in an impure land who are lax in both precepts and vehicle; those who are urgent in the vehicle but lax in precepts; those who are lax in the vehicle but diligent in precepts;
and those who are diligent in both precepts and vehicle.

[Commentary] Regarding the discussion of the precepts: among the ten precepts, only these four types—being unimpaired (*avikala*), unbroken (*abhagna*), unpierced (*achidra*), and untainted (*asamkīrṇa*)—are taken.

Of these four, the first three constitute the precept (*śīla*), while the latter one constitutes concentration (*samādhi*); both are causes for rebirth as humans or devas. The six types [of precepts] that follow the path, those praised by the non-attached wisdom (*anāsaṅga-jñāna*), those that are sovereign, and those that are fully endowed with concentration are not taken here.
Although these six are called the "essence of the precepts" (*śīla-svabhāva*), they are the third [category].

Contemplating that which belongs to the vehicles (*yāna*), one discusses the five vehicles. One does not include the human and celestial realms because, although these two are called "vehicles," they are neither moving nor emerging;
their essence consists of tainted wholesome states subsumed under ethical discipline (*śīla*). One includes only the three vehicles, as "śrāvaka" and so forth encompass the four teachings.
Although these are divided into deep and shallow levels regarding entry into principle and wisdom, all are capable of movement and emergence.

Because they involve afflictions and birth-and-death, they are termed "vehicles" (*yāna*); now, by correlating the four precepts with the three vehicles and discussing their relative urgency or laxity, four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established.
[Section on] "The Two Precepts are Urgent," which judges the retribution received.
When the precepts are urgent, one receives a human or celestial body; when the vehicle is urgent, there arises the capacity to respond to the sages.
[Commentary] "Precepts" refers to the past, while "capacity for response" refers to the present.
II. Regarding the capacities, the following clarifies the two faculties of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. A. First, a general clarification of how the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna respond to the Buddha.
There are two kinds of capacities: the great and the small. For those of small capacity, he manifests the body of a Buddha of the Tripitaka and preaches the Dharma;

for those of great capacity, he should manifest the body of the Śākyamuni Buddha (Vairocana) and preach the Dharma. Therefore, upon descending into his mother’s womb, he immediately displays these two aspects.

[Commentary] It is not that the matter of whether the precepts are maintained or violated is being questioned; rather, it is discussed solely in terms of practicing and studying the principle (*li*), whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna.
Therefore, within this text, the precepts are established to clarify the vehicle (*yāna*). As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "One whose precepts are lax is not yet called lax;
only one who is lax regarding the vehicle is truly called lax. This is because one who is lax in their precepts merely loses the realms of humans and devas, whereas if one is lax in the vehicle...
Regarding those who lacked the path to liberation and were divided between the Great and Small Vehicles:

those who formerly practiced contemplation for the sake of partial truth now constitute the small-capacity practitioners (*hīna-yānika*) who perceive only the form and voice of the Inferior Response Buddha (*hīna-nirmāṇa-buddha*).

Those who formerly practiced contemplation for the sake of the Middle Way now constitute the great-capacity practitioners (*mahā-yānika*) who can perceive the form and voice of the Superior Response Buddha (*viśiṣṭa-nirmāṇa-buddha*). As for the phrase "descending the spirit" and so forth, it refers to when the Tathāgata in the past...

Under the guidance of the Greatly Penetrating Buddha (*Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū*), he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and established the causes for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) for immeasurable sentient beings.

During that interval, some regressed from the Great Vehicle and became defiled by attachment to the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). Fearing they would fall into suffering, the Buddha subsequently rescued them through the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), or guided them using the three aspects of the Mahāyāna (*vaipulya*).
Thus, through various means of the Great and Small Vehicles, they were brought to maturity and are now fit for this present age.
To awaken to and enter the Buddha-vehicle, the Tathāgata appears in the world for this single purpose;
yet, because the capacities of sentient beings differ slightly, he divides his teaching into five periods throughout his lifetime.

There are those whose capacity allows them to enter directly into the ultimate reality, and those whose capacity can only enter the ultimate reality by way of a circuitous path. Although these two types mature at different times, they both reach fruition simultaneously.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, the sudden teaching discusses the perfect and distinct [vehicles] as they are applied to two types of capacities. These capacities have, from the very beginning, perceived the superior marks.

If, during the intervening period, one has practiced the Small Vehicle deeply, although such a person enters the One Buddha Vehicle in this present life, because the Small Vehicle matured first, for the sake of this capacity, a lowly body is manifested;
thus, the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka) were first taught, and through the various flavors of the teachings, they are gradually tamed and matured until they arrive at this stage.

The Lotus Sūtra alone opens the Buddha-wisdom; for those of this capacity, at the very beginning, he was seen only as one of inferior body, descending into his mother’s womb and manifesting two aspects.

Only after the sudden teaching of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra did he subsequently employ the gradual transformation of the Lesser Vehicle—just as a destitute son who cannot be reached by urgent pursuit will come when spoken to gently.
Thus, the principle of the initial suddenness followed by the subsequent gradualism is well established. Why, then, do you suddenly claim that [the Buddha] descended with a divine spirit?
The womb immediately manifests two aspects, as discussed in various texts: first, the sudden, and second, the gradual; these are merely provisional expressions regarding the methods of conversion.

What is explained here, however, shows that both the Great and Small Vehicles correspond [to the capacity of beings], ultimately returning to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) to fully exhaust the matter of discerning the beginning and end of their faculties.
As one contemplates the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paryāya*), there is no great capacity [for the Great Vehicle]; thus, the Buddhas intend to cease their transformative activity.
In the passage where it is stated that one first exhorts others before bestowing the *Hīnayāna*, the subsequent text says:

"For immeasurable kalpas I have praised the Dharma of *nirvāṇa* so that birth and death might be forever ended; I have always taught this. Therefore, one must contemplate the capacities of beings before bestowing the *Hīnayāna*.
Such statements are merely ritual conventions and cannot be used to challenge the present text, which foresees the various capacities of beings from their origins and essential principles.
This is the ultimate intent of saving sentient beings.
○ Second, specifically showing the benefits obtained by those of sudden capacity, divided into two parts: first, the characteristics of the benefit for those of great capacity.
What is perceived by those of sudden capacity is Śākyamuni Buddha (Śākyamuni Bodhisattva) surrounded by hundreds of thousands [of bodhisattvas], preaching the Dharma while dwelling within the womb.

All sentient beings of the ten directions are within the womb; when they emerge from the womb, the light of radiance fills the site of the tranquil extinction (śītinirvāṇa-maṇḍala), where they become Vairocana Buddha and turn the wheel of the Dharma of the single ultimate truth, the immeasurable four truths, and so forth. It is like the sun rising over a high mountain:
those in front are first illuminated, and upon hearing the Sudden Teaching, they perceive their Buddha-nature and attain liberation. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Like snow..."
"In the mountains there is a grass called 'Patience' (*kṣānti*); if an ox eats it, it immediately obtains the *sarpis-maṇḍa* (the finest essence of ghee). This is what that refers to.

[Commentary] A certain class of sentient beings has their "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) ripen first; they thus elicit a superior response, entering the womb, dwelling in the womb, emerging from the womb, and attaining Buddhahood—all these manifestations being superior.
This turns toward the Single True Reality (*ekābhisamaya-satya*), which is the *Avataṃsaka* section, the sudden teaching of the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇa-yāna*). Since...

Because it also includes the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), it is said to be "immeasurable. That sutra provides a preliminary overview of the beginning and end of the entire lifetime of the Buddha’s teaching, establishing a metaphor:
"It is like the rising sun, which first illuminates the high mountains, next illuminates the deep valleys, and finally illuminates the level plains.

According to the interpretation of our school, the "level plains" are further divided into three, corresponding to the five kinds of cow's milk flavors in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The "high mountains" represent those with great capacity who are able to evoke [the response of the Buddha].
In the Sunlight of the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*), when it shines before one, there is both gradual and non-gradual realization of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

If, in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the analogy of milk produced from a cow followed by the five flavors in sequence is used, this refers to the sequential arising of the flavors of the teachings across the five periods of the One Vehicle.
Now, to clarify that the capacity for sudden realization enables the vision of the Buddha-nature, the metaphor of eating grass is also employed.
The analogy is as follows: the Snowy Mountains represent Śākyamuni Buddha; the medicinal grasses represent the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
the ox eating represents the cultivation of contemplation by those of great capacity; and obtaining the clarified butter (ghṛta) immediately represents the realization of the Buddha-nature.

Commentary on the Meaning of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra, Scroll Four, composed by the Song dynasty Shramana Zhili of Siming. Section Two:
The Manner of Benefiting Beings of Lesser Capacity. Part Four: First, the Benefit of the Curdled Milk (Kṣīra); Sub-part One: Explaining the Response to Beings of Lesser Capacity.
If there are individuals of lesser capacity, they perceive the Buddha’s right mindfulness as entering the mother’s womb, being born in the royal palace, practicing austerities for six years,
sitting beneath the tree where he became an aged bhikṣu through the grass, and turning the Dharma wheel of the Four Truths of Arising and Cessation at the Deer Park so that the five men,
including Kauṇḍinya, first attained the nectar of immortality and realized the path of the Hīnayāna.
[Commentary] These are those among the small class whose seeds ripened first; they initially attained the inferior *śrāvaka* fruit.
From their entry into the womb until their attainment of Buddhahood, their characteristics were all inferior. Kūṭadanta, Kauṇḍinya, or Kauṇḍinyaputra—these five were the leaders.
As for the other four, namely Abhibhū, Mahānāman, and the Prince Kolita, at the very beginning...
Realizing the principle of the Four Noble Truths at the Deer Park is called "attaining the ambrosia"; this was the Buddha-sun’s next illumination of the dark valleys.
○ Second, "Since it is not... and so forth, which provides a grand discrimination against [other teachings]. Part one: advancing to discriminate the awakening from the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Since it is neither the *amṛta* (nectar) nor yet called "attaining deliverance," it is said that merely being free from delusion is termed "liberation";
in reality, one has not yet attained all-encompassing liberation.

[Commentary] Although the path of the initial teaching is called "ambrosia" (*amṛta*), since it is not yet the flavor of the fifth stage, the *amṛta* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), how could it be so?
Because they have crossed over two kinds of birth and death but have not yet been called "attained liberation," the phrase "and so forth" cites this sutra.

Although they have used a single gate to liberate themselves from the bonds of false views and afflictions (*kleśa*), they have in fact not yet attained liberation from all objective realms or from the delusions and entanglements of *moha* as numerous as motes of dust;
it is only upon reaching Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa that they will finally realize this liberation.
II. Regarding those who are not yet capable [of receiving the Great Teaching], there are two parts:

first, the section on being like the milk of Mahānāman, which explains that they are like the deaf or mute regarding the Great Teaching and thus derive no benefit from it; however, within the Great Teaching, there exists the power of subtle, latent influence (*mīng-xūn*), which is illustrated by the analogy of milk.

[Commentary] Here, the fact that those who had already realized the Small Vehicle did not hear the Great [Vehicle] upon encountering it is used to verify that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) were incapable of receiving the Great [Vehicle].
Although the text regarding their deafness and muteness appears in the latter part of the sutra, the time [of its occurrence] was still long;

thus, in meaning, this corresponds to the period of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings, though it may also be understood as preceding the Deer Park [teachings]. For this reason, Kāśyapa subsequently describes the capacities of those with Small Vehicle predispositions.
When he was first exposed to the Great [Vehicle], he was bewildered and fell to the ground; later, it became manifest that his faculties had not yet been able to sustain it.

Although there was indeed hidden benefit, how could it have remedied the fact that the afflictions of attachment were still actively manifest? Thus, his faculties remained entirely immature within the *Avataṃsaka*, like milk.
[Commentary]: Second, upon hearing the means [of liberation], one descends from the minor stage and names it "curd" (*dadhi*).
When one hears the skillful means for severing the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) within the three realms, at that moment milk is transformed and named "curd.

[Record]: One who pursues urgently and pays back wealth is called a "complainant" and cries out loudly; one who speaks slowly while clearing away filth is joyful and follows along, and thus is given [the gift].
Using skillful means, he taught the suffering of the three realms; because they feared this suffering, they severed the accumulation of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa-samudaya*).
Having thus transformed their state from ordinary to holy, it is called "transforming milk into curd.
Second, they next hear of "lower ghee" (*apakva-manda*).

Next, hearing the Vaipulya [teachings]—the fourfold Four Noble Truths that use the Great to critique the Small, feeling shame for the provisional and longing for the real, and giving rise to a heart of profound reverence—is called "produced ghee. [Commentary:

All four teachings are expounded together to horizontally encompass the various capacities of sentient beings; when those of small capacity hear the critiques and rebukes, they gradually become able to long for the Great, secretly attaining [realization].
It benefits bodhisattvas of dull faculties and benefits those equal to the two vehicles; by harmonizing these capacities, one attains the flavor of "fresh butter" (*navanīta*).

It should be understood that when clarifying the five flavors according to the teachings, one does not take into account their intensity or dilution, but speaks only of their sequential arising, because sudden milk is itself the *amṛta* (clarified butter).

If, however, one considers them according to the capacities [of the practitioners], there is the sense of intensity and dilution; yet this refers specifically to the most dull among those of the three vehicles.
It is said that for this particular class of beings, the *Avataṃsaka* provides no benefit at all—just as milk mixed with blood and raw meat cannot become curd when the Tripitaka is taught;
rather, for such a faculty, it becomes curd and gradually thickens until it reaches its ultimate flavor.
Third, one hears the "matured ghee" (pakva-sarpis).
Next, by hearing the three types of the Four Noble Truths as taught through the *Prajñāpāramitā*, one's mind becomes somewhat purified; this is called "matured ghee.

[Commentary] This does not refer to those who enter the Perfect [Vehicle] from the Three Baskets (*Tripiṭaka*), but rather to those of sharp faculties among the Śrāvakas who enter the Perfect [Vehicle] after having fully demonstrated the three benefits of the Mahāyāna.
Having reached this point, the teaching was further transformed; since it fully expounds the myriad practices within the true void, those of dull faculties attain a hidden, specific benefit.
In terms of training gradual-capacity practitioners, this is called the flavor of "matured butter" (*pakva-ghṛta*).
○ Fourth, hearing the *Amṛta* (the finest cream) below. 1. First, regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*: 2. First, clarifying that those of the three vehicles all attain Buddhahood.
Next, upon hearing the *Lotus Sūtra*, they abandon the three provisional means; however, when only the Buddha’s single true knowledge and vision are taught, the Śrāvakas harbor doubts.

Except for those bodhisattvas who have received the prediction of Buddhahood—who eliminate delusions, advance on the path, and diminish births—at that time they are called *amṛta* (clarified butter) bodhisattvas and may go everywhere;

those of dull faculties are likewise [treated] as the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). As for those of the two vehicles, it is only from this point onward that they are able to perceive the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
[Commentary] Having set aside the four truths of the expedient means of the three previous teachings, [the Buddha] speaks only of the one true, unsurpassed Way;

yet he further opens the gates of the expedient means of the three teachings—all of which are the true aspect of the One Vehicle. This is precisely what is meant by the two kinds of marvelous discourse—of "provisional" and "ultimate"—in this sutra.
Because it speaks of this marvel, it causes the two vehicles to be like parched grain that is made to sprout again, and causes the bodhisattvas of the three teachings to attain rebirth.
Since provisional [teachings] and doubt have eternally ceased, there is not a single one who does not attain Buddhahood.
Second, the passage beginning with "Therefore it is said" provides proof that all within the One Lifetime enter the *tathāgatagarbha* (the nectar of immortality).
Thus it says: "As soon as they see my body and hear what I preach, they all believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata. This is the realization.
Those of great capacity who previously attained the *amṛta* (the essence of enlightenment)— excluding those who had first practiced and studied the Hīnayāna—
I now likewise cause to hear this sutra so that they may enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata; thus, those of small capacity begin their entry into the *amṛta* at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

[Commentary] If those of great capacity have first matured, they enter the Buddha-wisdom immediately upon seeing the *Avataṃsaka*; if those of small capacity have first matured, they must be led gradually.

Now, by hearing the teaching on the opening and the setting aside [of provisional teachings], one finally attains the Buddha-wisdom. What was initially attained and what is now attained are both the Buddha-wisdom;
both are likened to the *amṛta* (clarified butter), yet while the former includes the distinct [teachings], this [latter] is purely perfect.
Second, regarding "if one further descends into nirvana":

if there are those of dull faculties who do not awaken to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* but instead undergo further refinement through the *Prajñāpāramitā* until they reach nirvana, it is explained that the three superior practices lead to the realization of the eternal abiding and the vision of the Buddha-nature; this is the *amṛta* (the finest essence).

[Commentary] The intent of revelation is fully manifested in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Having already defeated the great army of those sentient beings who cling to provisional teachings, it was still necessary to gather in their remaining followers through the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Therefore, following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā* was further taught to refine their minds so that they might attain the flavor of the "ghee" (amṛta) within *nirvāṇa*.
For this reason, that scripture is summarized at the conclusion of the *Prajñā* section.
Regarding the sequence of the five flavors, it is said that the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* emerges from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and explains the "superior threefold cultivation.
That sutra clarifies three types of threefold cultivation: first, the false; second, the inferior; and third, the superior.

The "false" refers to that which is taught by worldly false teachers as permanence, bliss, and self. The "inferior" refers to relying on the Buddha’s partial teaching to break through false attachments, namely [the realization of] impermanence.
There is no pleasure and no self; rather, by relying on the supreme teaching of the Buddha, one refutes inferior cultivation—namely, the notions of permanence, pleasure, and self.
The Dharma-body is eternal and unchanging; it wanders among the blossoms of awakening, enjoying bliss and possessing the eight masteries that cannot be obstructed.
One who cultivates in this manner enters the Secret Treasury; this is called the superior threefold cultivation.
The second part consists of two sections: first, establishing the example of the Buddha’s body;
this refers to manifesting the Buddha-body in the defiled land of the Shared Residence to preach the Perfect and Gradual Dharma.
Second, "Alternatively, he manifests... and so forth, which serves as an example for the other bodies.
Alternatively, manifesting various bodies to preach the Dharma of the Perfect and the Gradual—these four phrases open up the meaning of the five flavors.

[Commentary: Since the Buddha-body is capable of preaching the teachings of the five periods, if he manifests other bodies, he likewise leads those of true practice through the five periods, turning according to the flavor.
Furthermore, one must discuss the manifestation of many bodies to deliver a single person, or...
Since the cases of "one time, many" or "one time, one" and "many times, many" regarding persons are thus established,

and since the four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) are each formed by correlating the relative quantities of persons, dharmas, causes, and effects, I shall first provide a preliminary outline by establishing these three or four permutations before fully expounding the characteristics of response and transformation (*saṃdarśana*).
○ Third, the defiled land serves as an example for the pure land.

Since it is so with the defiled land, it is likewise with the pure land. As there are both sharp and dull faculties among sentient beings, how could there not be the two teachings of sudden and gradual to clarify the manifestation of the response-body and its preaching of the Dharma?

[Commentary]: Just as there are countless bodhisattvas in the Land of Peace and Bliss, so it is with the śrāvakas; this is because the Dharma has both sudden and gradual aspects, and thus people are divided into the Great and Small Vehicles.
As detailed in the *Nine Grades of Rebirth*, after being born in that land, they enter the stages of the Great or Small Vehicles;

this is known through experience to result from hearing the Dharma. It should be understood that for those who deliver sentient beings in that Pure Land, two kinds of bodies—the gradual and the sudden—must be discussed.
[The text] says:
"2. Within this, [the practitioner] contemplates the fundamental contemplation of compassion.

Here, one should clarify the compassion arising from the fundamental contemplations of the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles]; now, the way it arises throughout the entire dharma-realm should be illustrated accordingly."
As previously stated, etc. [Commentary]:

As clarified above, the manifestation of forms in the three lands to transform sentient beings across the five periods—whereby the defiled refers to Śākyamuni and the pure refers to Amitābha—is fully manifested in the scriptural texts of these two Buddhas’ transformative activities, thereby revealing the appearance of the Buddha-body by Avalokiteśvara.
Since this is not a partial realization, its ultimate essence and function are identical; if the resultant function is thus, how could it lack a fundamental cause?

Therefore, we now trace back to the original: at the time of practicing the distinct and perfect contemplations, one gave rise to compassionate vows, vowing to manifest throughout the Dharma-realm to preach the Dharma and deliver all sentient beings.
Now, abiding in the Land of Quiescent Light, these original vows are fulfilled.

The manner in which that which is perfumed pervades the three lands through forms, sounds, and benefits has already been fully explained in the preceding section on "Responding to Calamities" within the text of the Original Vow.
○ Third, the question regarding the names and essences of the lands below; Part Two: First, distinguishing the names of the lands; First, the question.
Question: The sutra merely states that [the Buddha] "wanders through the Sahā world," and does not mention the Real Reward Land, the Land of Expedient Means, or other lands.

[Commentary]: The name "Sahā" is translated as "Endurance. Since this term does not even apply to the Pure Land within the Shared Residence (Tongju) land, how can it possibly be explained by encompassing all three lands?
II. The Response.
In the general response, it says: "Wandering through various lands"—since these are not one, how could they refer to the Sahā world alone?
Furthermore, as the *Mahāvaipulya* Sūtra states: "If one can deeply contemplate and see me on Vulture Peak together with the assembly..."
Hearing of the Bodhisattva Saṃgha here in this Sahā world is itself a skillful means;

furthermore, it is said that seeing me as consisting purely of bodhisattvas, with no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, is the true retribution land. Therefore, there is no fault in clarifying the meaning by way of these two lands.
[Commentary: The Bodhisattva raises a single point as the opening of the question, while the Tathāgata provides an answer based on the all-pervasiveness of the Dharma.

Thus it is said that he "travels through various lands in manifold forms," crossing horizontally throughout the ten directions and penetrating vertically through the three lands; hence the term "various" (zhū).
These are all the locations where the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) of Avalokiteśvara dwells. This [answer] exceeds the question in accordance with the text provided by the Tathāgata.

This is the explanation. Furthermore, if one examines this according to its meaning, its characteristics are perfectly clear. Why? Because the sutra demonstrates that the land of skillful means and the land of true retribution are not separate from Sahā;

thus it says: "If one hears of the long life [of the Buddha] and believes and understands it with a profound mind, then one shall see the Buddha constantly on Vulture Peak, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, preaching the Dharma. Since...
It is said that while Yaśas was always on Mount Vaideha, the kalpa-fire blazed fiercely yet this land remained peaceful;
furthermore, with bodhisattvas and śrāvakas together serving as the audience, is this not the Sahā world itself as a land of skillful means?
Again, it is said that he saw the Sahā world where its ground was made of lapis lazuli and even its towers and pavilions were entirely composed of jewels—such were those bodhisattvas.
Since it is said that the multitude all dwell within it and yet see it, this is not merely the previous location;

rather, it is because the Bodhisattvas alone—unshared with Śrāvakas—constitute a Saṃgha consisting purely of Bodhisattvas. Thus we verify that the Sahā world is itself the Land of True Reward (*vipākaphala-bhūmi*).
These passages all concern the wondrous contemplation of the four faiths, whereby one perceives two lands within the Saha world through the profound wisdom of Avalokiteśvara.
How could one who wanders through the Sahā world permit themselves to dwell alone in such a defiled realm?
II. Second, the question; second, below, the clarification of the essence of the land. 1. First, the question.
Question: Since both are equally termed "Dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena), how can they be different?
[Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that outside the triple world there is a Pure Land where Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are born;
they receive the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*) rather than being born through the process of segmented birth (*pariccheda-jāti*), which refers to the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states that the Dharma-body Buddha preaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-nature body, and that the assembly listening to the Dharma consists not of those subject to birth and death, but merely says...

The bodhisattva’s non-common [realm] with the two vehicles is precisely the Land of True Reward (*sambhoga-kṣetra*). Since these two lands are distinct yet both are termed *dharmatā*, how are they to be distinguished?
[The second part: The answer.
Answer: This differs greatly from the Middle Way of the Satyasiddhi-śāstra. [Commentary:
The Hinayana theory of "extinction like ashes" asserts that there is no rebirth beyond the realms; yet it speaks of "leaving the realms" and then "receiving a body.
This is based on the Mahayana perspective. The Dharma-nature of the Mahayana is inherently and eternally abiding, serving as the source of all form and mind. How could this be so?

The "lesser" [teaching] holds that the causes of form and mind exist because of view-delusion (*dṛṣṭi*) and affliction-delusion (*kleśa*); thus, when the bonds of these causes are severed, their effects are forever forgotten.
The "greater" [teaching] states that form and mind arise from delusion and undergo cessation; they do not possess a substantial nature independent of delusion, for their essence is *dharmatā*.

If view-delusion and affliction-delusion are exhausted while ignorance (*avidyā*) remains entirely intact, then the form and mind of *dharmatā* as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) are subject to conventional arising and ceasing, while ignorance is only partially broken.

In the sense that the fundamental nature is manifested, the Middle Way of the Dharma-nature (dharmatā) consists of the true retribution of form and mind, wherein birth and death and ignorance are thoroughly exhausted;
thus, the fundamental nature is eternally abiding, and form and mind are free from the marks of saṃsāra—this is the eternal tranquil light.

Herein, we clarify that although the names "expedient means" (upāya) and "true retribution land" (vipākabhūmi) regarding the Dharma-nature are the same, there is a great difference when discussed in terms of the severing of delusions within the ultimate truth.
Section Two: Explaining the Manifested Bodhisattvas. Part One: Explaining the Manifested Aspects. Subsection One: The Differences in How They Assist the Buddha.

Next, explaining that those who are to be saved by means of a manifested bodhisattva—whether they belong to a higher or lower stage, or whether they are of the Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, or Perfect teachings—differ in how they assist the Buddha.
For instance, if the Buddha manifests as a Buddha in the Stage of True Reward (*bhūtaniṣyanda-bhūmi*), Avalokiteśvara then appears as a bodhisattva of that same stage of true reward.
He manifests either in the form of a Bodhisattva in the *upāya-bhūmi* (Land of Expedient Means) or in the form of a Bodhisattva in the *sahā-bhūmi* (Land of Common Dwelling),
responding to the two types of conditions— those of sharp and dull faculties.
[Commentary] Discussing the four teachings horizontally, and the three lands vertically, each land has its own presiding teacher, and each of the four teachings likewise has its own.

The Bodhisattvas assist and support the transformative mechanisms through two teachings—expedient means and the true reward—and one perfect teaching; in each case, the Bodhisattvas must assist the Buddha by adapting to the conditions of sentient beings.
Second, regarding "responding to benefit," there are differences in how they respond to conditions.
Those who respond to sharp conditions are like Fahuì (Dharmamati) and Jingangzang (Vajragarbha) in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; those who respond to dull conditions are like Maitreya and others.
When the Buddha turns the Dharma-gates of the five flavors, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who assist him also arise and cease at each successive stage;
whether through provisional or ultimate means, they extensively benefit sentient beings.

[Commentary] To summarize briefly, the sudden teaching is for those of sharp faculties, while the gradual teaching is for those of dull faculties. However, if one were to discuss this in detail, there are cases where the sudden teaching contains the dull, and the gradual teaching contains the sharp.
The dharmas taught arise or cease according to the capacities of sentient beings, and the auxiliary teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas likewise undergo transformation accordingly;
it is impossible to record them all in writing, so one should reflect upon them in accordance with the teachings.
II. From "In this regard" onwards, the brief exposition of the chapter on the fundamental contemplation of the Buddha is clarified.
Within this, one should also clarify the distinct and perfect fundamental contemplations regarding the capacity and response.
III. The Branch Buddhas.

Next, to clarify those who should be [taught] as Pratyekabuddhas: for example, Mañjuśrī acted as a Pratyekabuddha for twenty-two billion kalpas to transform sentient beings, manifesting his body and preaching the Dharma.

[Commentary: If one discusses the Pratyekabuddha who is solitary, since he does not encounter a Buddha and receives no instruction, how could he preach the Dharma with the intent to transform sentient beings?
However, while manifesting supernatural transformations, he now speaks of the Dharma; this refers to those who received the teachings on causes and conditions during the Buddha's lifetime.
This clarifies that [the Buddha] provisionally manifested [these forms] to lead those of similar kind, turning according to their inclinations just as with the śrāvakas.
The fourth section clarifies the śrāvakas below [the bodhisattvas], in two parts: first, it clarifies those who are manifested;
second, it clarifies those who should appear in the form of śrāvakas—whether as those of the Tripiṭaka, those of the Shared Teaching, or those śrāvakas who transform according to the five flavors.
II. Internally secret, the following clarifies that the manifestation is identical in all respects to the actual practice;
now it is clarified that this manifestation is known to be a great expedient means (*mahopāya*). Within this, there are four parts; first, the intention of the manifestation.
Internally secret and externally manifesting, he adorns the four withering and the four flourishing to guide sentient beings.
[Commentary] He externally displays provisional traces, his intent being to adorn the twin trees of Nirvana. Regarding the "twin trees," there are two pairs in each of the four directions;
in the east, one pair consists of one withering tree and one flourishing tree, and it is likewise so in the south, west, and north. In the east...

The east represents flourishing and decay, as well as permanence and impermanence; the south represents pleasure and the absence of pleasure; the west represents self and non-self; and the north represents purity and impurity.
The Tathāgata lay with his head toward the north and entered parinirvāṇa, thereby signifying the transcendence of both permanence and impermanence, and so forth.
The scriptural text briefly mentions six individuals from the causal stage: namely, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Subhūti, and Aniruddha.
Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and one person who has attained the fruit—this is the Tathāgata himself. These are all well able to adorn the twin trees.
This is because the Tathāgata and Śāriputra and the others have long since realized the three virtues (*triguṇa*), desiring to cause sentient beings to enter the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*).

Since the twin trees are neither permanent nor impermanent, they are the true four virtues (*caturguṇa*). Therefore, at the beginning, the primary and attendant figures of the Tripiṭaka were together in harmony.
Those who practice with earnest application and realize impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity constitute the "four kinds of withered trees.
Next, regarding the two *sūtras* (the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Nirvāṇa*), they praise the Perfect [Teaching], disparage the Partial, reproach the Small, and admire the Great;

by preaching the Bodhisattva Dharma, they lead all sentient beings to shatter their attachment to impermanence and cultivate the study of permanence and so forth—these constitute the "four kinds of flourishing trees. This continues until the assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the present time.

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*—which leads all sentient beings to equally realize and enter the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Middle Way characterized by the four virtues, being neither withered nor flourishing—demonstrates that the merit of the primary and attendant teachings throughout the entire lifetime of the Buddha’s ministry has now been fulfilled.
It is therefore manifested through his entry into nirvana between the twin trees; thus it is said: "The six classes of beings and the Tathāgata together adorn the twin trees."
The intention behind the tree-āśoka manifesting in the form of a śrāvaka is as follows.
Second, it introduces the person who can manifest [the transformation];
next, it cites from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* how various bodhisattvas and bhikṣus enter the dharma-realm and behold the dwelling in the inconceivable.
The "Dharma-gate" (dharmaparyāya) is that which accomplishes this meaning.

[Commentary] The various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) seen by Sudhana—such as the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha and the bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita—manifested the bodies of śrāvakas and preached the distinct and perfect teachings (*bhedavibuddha* and *paripūrṇa*).
When those with the faculties of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) made their appeal, he preached the *pitaka* of the *āgama* and *vaipulya*. Since they had already abided in the inconceivable...
In what Dharma-gate has this not been expounded? This now accords with the four phrases of the "Wenren" (Literati) Dharma.
Third, it cites the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] on the ability to manifest the Dharma;
next, it cites the four kinds of contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, namely the distinct, the perfect, the original ground, and compassion.
"Taking up and not abandoning" now constitutes the four kinds of noble ones who universally respond to all.
[Commentary: Above, this was a general discussion of the Dharma to manifest those capable of appearing; here, it specifically demonstrates the skillful means of the Small Vehicle.

Therefore, it cites the four kinds of wisdom from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*: by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, one attains the fruits of the four vehicles. If Avalokiteśvara practices these individually...

In the sequential contemplation (*anupūrva-vipaśyanā*), one employs the four wisdoms to contemplate conditions; however, in the perfect contemplation (*yuganaddha-vipaśyanā*), one employs the wisdom of the four causal conditions within a single mind.
In each instance, one gives rise to vows to deliver all sentient beings, neither grasping at the four marks nor abandoning the four dharmas.
Because of non-grasping, there is no existence; because of non-abandoning, there is no emptiness. By simultaneously negating both extremes, one enters the Middle Way.
Based on the vows, the two—birth and phenomena—are simultaneously illuminated; these are the four types of compassion.

Now that the practice and vows are fulfilled, they manifest in four forms throughout the Dharma-realm, universally responding to all beings. Among these four, the wisdom of equality is taken as the agent that manifests the phenomena.
IV. Four Questions, Part Two: Entrusting a Comparative Analysis. First, the Question. Question:
You say, "How does the Buddha save?

[Commentary]: This arises from the preceding analysis that the bodies of the ten realms respond to the capacities of the ten realms, such that the one and the many interpenetrate and are thus established.
The four-line verse concludes with the statement that because there is a Buddha who delivers beings within the Buddha-realm, this present question arises.
II. The Response.

The response concerns the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) manifesting a Buddha-body to deliver those on the First Ground. What is the intention behind [the claim] that he cannot be like an ordinary human being?
"Able to deliver beings" (and so forth).
[Commentary] The answer states that "the Perfectly Awakened One delivers those on the first stage" is according to the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).

This is because the meaning of the six stages of "immediate Buddhahood" (*liuji*) in the Perfect Teaching is too broad, whereas the meaning of the Buddha-realm upon ascending the stages in the Distinct Teaching is manifest. Why? Because the three levels of worthiness (*sanxian*) in the Distinct Teaching are employed...
The contemplative methods cultivated by those of the Three Vehicles lead to entry into the stages (*bhūmi*) and realization within the Middle Way;

they transcend the nine realms and, through the integration of the fundamental and the derivative, as well as essence and function, become identical to the Buddha. Nevertheless, because this is but a partial realization, afflictions necessarily vary in thickness and wisdom in depth.

Therefore, while the Buddhas who manifest transformation for others at higher stages deliver those at lower stages, the Buddhas of one's own practice serve as an analogy to a human teacher delivering his disciples.
Disciples must know that the Buddhas who are able to deliver others may manifest the eight phases of enlightenment or sit upon the King of Flowers;

however, the Buddhas who deliver others necessarily manifest as causal bodies (*hetu-kāya*), for they do not rely on the formal characteristics of the Dharma (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) in their Buddha-dignity. Thus, the Buddhas of all four teachings possess unlearned wisdom (*asikṣita-jñāna*).

Furthermore, for the time being, it is said that those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) deliver those on the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*); yet, if one considers the fundamental [reality], the trace is high.

It may be said that [the Buddha] traverses from the first stage up to Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) to manifest the traces of a Buddha; this is because the body of Sublime Enlightenment (mi-jo-kyō-shin) results from the empowerment of the ultimate fruit.
To those who should be saved by the body of a Brahmā King, he manifests as a Brahmā King and preaches the Dharma for them; to those who should be saved by [the body of] an Indra...
To those who are to be delivered by the body of Śakra, he manifests the body of Śakra and preaches the Dharma for them;
to those who are to be delivered by the body of Īśvara, he manifests the body of Īśvara and preaches the Dharma for them;
to those who are to be delivered by the body of Maheśvara, he manifests the body of Maheśvara and preaches the Dharma for them; to those who are to be delivered by the body of a Heavenly General...
To those who are to be delivered through the form of a celestial general, he manifests as a celestial general and preaches the Dharma to them;
to those who are to be delivered through the form of Vaiśravaṇa, he manifests as Vaiśravaṇa and preaches the Dharma to them.
II. Clarifying the Bodies of the Lower Heavens (6): First, the Brahmā King. 1. Explaining the Name and Characteristics; 2. Clarifying the Brahmā Body. Regarding "Brahmā":
this is the name of the Lord of the Rūpadhātu, translated as *Śikhin* (Topknot), meaning "Crest-Jewel.
This clarifies that there is a king for each of the four dhyānas. The term used here, "Brahmā," likely refers to the summit of the first dhyāna, which still possesses vitarka (applied thought).
By contemplating the dharma of speech, one attains the status of lord over a thousand worlds.
Second, from "Contemplating Avalokiteśvara" downward, this clarifies the fundamental contemplation.
Contemplating Avalokiteśvara, one cultivates the white-colored samādhi; because it is neither grasped nor abandoned, and because it is not grasped, one does not follow the rebirths of the dhyānas.

Having relinquished [the previous state], he should act as the Brahma King and expound the four-line discourse on the transcendence of desire; manifesting his body through skillful means, he leads others toward the ultimate reality.

[Commentary]: This deity’s environment and inhabitants (*āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*) are predominantly white. When Avalokiteśvara contemplates the white color during the causal stage, it is immediately empty, provisional, and middle.
Abiding within the White Dharma-realm (*śukla-dharmadhātu*), this very existence possesses the nature of true permanence and self, which is called the "King Samādhi" (*Rāja-samādhi*).
To "take up but not abandon" means: not taking up the mark of existence (*sanimitta*) in this dhyāna refers to the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);

not taking up the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatānimitta*) in this dhyāna refers to the *pāramitā-śata-sahasra*; and not taking up the marks of both existence and non-existence (*ubhayanimitta*) or neither existence nor non-existence (*anubhayanimitta*) in this dhyāna refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus, one does not follow the three delusions to be born within this dhyāna or the three lands (*tridhātu-bhūmi*). Because they are not abandoned, it is precisely...
He is able to manifest in response as a Brahmā King dwelling together with ordinary beings;
he is also able to manifest in response as a Brahmā King of Expedient Means, as the Āgamas state that one who has already realized the third fruit is about to enter the Land of Expedient Means;

furthermore, he is able to manifest in response as a Brahmā King of Real Reward, as the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Renwang jing) states that this refers to the realization of the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). He also expounds the *Treatise on the Departure from Desire*, wherein "desire" refers to the three delusions.
The manifestation of the body through the four propositions consists of the relative relationship between one and many, thereby forming these four propositions.

This is done by using provisional means to lead toward the ultimate reality, guiding those who practice in the three lands. As detailed in the section on the Buddha below, all manifestations of the various bodies should be understood according to this same principle.
○ Second, Śakra.
Those who should appear in the body of Śakra are the lords of the earth-dwelling deities;
their full name is Śakradevānām-indra. "Śakra" means "able"; "devānām" refers to the gods (*deva*); and "indra" is... [the lord].
The Bodhisattva named Lord Capable of Action (Nāthaśaktikara) cultivates the Samādhi Difficult to Subdue;
he neither grasps nor abandons, expounds various superior discourses on the four propositions, and manifests his body through skillful means to lead beings toward the ultimate reality.
Third, the Heaven of Mastery (Vaśavartin).
This is the pinnacle of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). It is called *Paranirmita-vaśavartin*, which means "Mastery over the Creations of Others";

that is, one achieves one's own pleasures by utilizing the creations of others. This is precisely the Demon King (*māra-rāja*). As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "For the most part, this is not..."
The Bodhisattva of Contemplative Liberation dwells in the Crimson Samādhi;

neither grasping nor rejecting, he should act as a Māra-king, causing all realms of Māra to be identical to the realm of the Buddha, manifesting in four modes of appearance to use skillful means to lead beings toward the ultimate reality.
○ Mastery over the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Mahesvara is the Lord Maheśvara at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), whom the *Loutan jing* calls Akaniṣṭha and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* calls Akaniṣṭha-bhavana (the Ultimate Form).
Some consider him to be [the lord] of the sixth heaven, yet various sūtras...
Many treatises refer to Maheśvara as the pinnacle of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states:

"Beyond the Śuddhāvāsakāyika deities, there are Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) named Maheśvara, who are lords of the trichiliocosm. The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "The radiance of the Maheśvara deity surpasses that of all sentient beings;
because the Maheśvara deity is most supreme, [offerings are presented to him in the *Nirvāṇa*]. This is not [the case].
The *Commentary on the Sixth Heaven* states: "Maheśvara is here called Mahādeva; he rides a white ox, has eight arms and three eyes, and is the general of all the devas.
It is not yet known whether this refers to the same person, or whether it specifically designates the King as the general.
○ The Great Generals of the Five Heavens.
Regarding the Heavenly Great Generals, according to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, it is Sanjaya who serves as the Great General.

The aforementioned great sūtra states that there are eight *kumbhāṇḍas* who are warriors among the gods; the *Śāstra* refers to Maheśvara as such, and as mentioned previously, it also refers to Kūṣmāṇḍa.
*Maga* is translated here as "Child"; he rides a peacock, holds a cock, carries a bell, and grasps a red banner. *Vaiśravaṇa* is called "Universal Renown" (*Pienwen*);
he has four arms, holds a conch and a treatise, and rides a golden-winged bird (*garuḍa*). These are all great generals of the devas;
it remains unknown which of these great generals this one specifically is. [These] four lines form a parallel couplet.
[Commentary] The omission of Vaiśravaṇa is because he is already visible [to the world].
Those who are to be saved by the body of a minor king, he immediately manifests as a minor king and preaches the Dharma for them;

those who are to be saved by the body of an elder (śreṣṭhin), he immediately manifests as an elder and preaches the Dharma for them; those who are to be saved by the body of a householder (gṛhapati)...
To those who are to be saved by appearing in the form of a layperson (*gṛhapati*), he appears in the body of a layperson and preaches the Dharma to them;

to those who are to be saved by appearing in the body of a minister (*kṣatriya*), he appears in the body of a minister and preaches the Dharma to them; to those who are to be saved by appearing in the body of a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*), he appears in the body of a Brahmin and preaches the Dharma to them.

III. The Bodies of Lesser Kings and Below. Part Five: First, the Lesser Kings. Regarding the body of a lesser king: some say that among heavenly kings there are great and small, and among human kings there are likewise four types of Cakravartin (Wheel-Turning) kings who have their own degrees of greatness and smallness; those who are not Cakravartins are called *kṣudraka-rāja* (scattered or minor kings). Regarding the body of a lesser king: some say that among heavenly kings there are great and small, and among human kings there are likewise four types of Cakravartin kings who have their own degrees of greatness and smallness; those who are not Cakravartins are called *kṣudraka-rāja*. Among these human kings, there are four kinds of Cakravartin kings who possess their own distinctions of magnitude and minuteness; those who do not belong to the four classes of Cakravartins are termed *kṣudraka-rāja* (minor or scattered kings). They are so named because they rule over small territories and possess limited power.
